reports.summary: Prior art shows GPUs win at compression only when the format is laid out for them (nvCOMP LZ4/Snappy with a warp per 64 KiB chunk, GDeflate's 32 interleaved sub-streams, interleaved-state ANS as in dietgpu, ACEAPEX absolute offsets) or when a stage is a bulk sort or prefix-sum (BWT, iBWT). Formats KaitoKit and GyoshukuKit actually handle (Deflate, bzip2, LZMA/LZMA2, zstd, LZ4 frames) carry serial dependencies inside each block, so a GPU thread must walk them serially. Measured on this M4 Max, one GPU thread runs an identical table-lookup decode loop at 10 MB/s versus 600 MB/s for one P-core (60:1), and the GPU reaches its ~180-200 GB/s aggregate only with 20,000 or more concurrently active independent streams; a 1 GB archive of 900 kB bzip2 blocks or 4 MiB LZ4 blocks supplies 250-1,200, so per-block serial GPU decode lands at 0.2-10 GB/s and loses to, or at best ties, 12 P-cores plus 4 E-cores. The CPU bars are high: this machine does zlib CRC-32 at 46 GB/s per core and 243 GB/s on 16 lanes with crc32_combine, AES-128-CTR at 18.5 GB/s per core and 142 GB/s on 16 lanes, gzip -d 1.6 GB/s, zstd -d 1.9 GB/s, lz4 -d 2.8 GB/s, xz -d 322 MB/s, bzip2 -d 78 MB/s per core, and the GPU's own measured copy bandwidth is only 369 GB/s, so CRC and AES on the GPU can tie but never beat the CPU. Metal itself is adequate for these kernels (32 KiB threadgroup memory, SIMD-group permute/reduction/ballot, 32-bit atomics, zero-copy MTLBuffer over 16 KiB-aligned CPU memory) with two measured caveats: an empty command buffer costs 146 µs round-trip, so each dispatch must carry tens of MB, and 64-bit device atomics do not compile in the runtime MSL headers on macOS 27.2 despite the feature table saying Apple9 has them. Encode-side offloads (GPU LZ77 match finding, GPU forward BWT) are blocked not by throughput but by the fact that every encoder in the two repos is a closed library (zlib deflate, libbz2, Apple Compression LZMA) with no hook for external matches or sorts; only the small LH5 encoder is in-house. Recommendation: try first the one decode case with a realistic chance, warp-per-block LZ4 frame decoding of block-independent frames (the lz4 CLI default: measured FLG B.Indep=1, 4 MiB blocks), against a 16-lane libcompression baseline, and in the same demo fuse CRC-32 into the kernel as a by-product; write the report's CRC-32 and AES sections first as measured "why the CPU wins" results, and treat GPU bzip2 decode (fine-grained iBWT, ICPP'24 style) as the second experiment only if the LZ4 demo shows the GPU pipeline overhead is under control. Beating the in-house Swift zstd decoder (197 MB/s) or PPMd (14 MB/s) with a GPU would prove nothing; those gaps are CPU optimisation work against libzstd's 1.9 GB/s.

candidates.name: LZ4 frame block-parallel decode (warp per block, nvCOMP style)
candidates.whatItComputes: Decodes each independent LZ4 block (KaitoKit LZ4FrameDecompressor / LZ4BlockDecoder input) with one SIMD-group: lanes parse token/literal-length/offset cooperatively, literal copies and match copies are spread across the 32 lanes with a threadgroup-memory staging window, blocks are independent so no cross-block state.
candidates.mapping: Fits the SIMD-group model: nvCOMP and nvCOMPDx decode one 64 KiB chunk per warp with lanes doing vectorised copies; the serial part is only the token parse, which the 2026 H100 study measures at 64-72% of decode time even there. Memory: a 4 MiB block does not fit 32 KiB threadgroup memory, so copies go through device memory (unified, zero-copy) and rely on L2. Precision: pure 8/32-bit integer work, no 64-bit atomics needed. The catch is parallelism: LZ4 frames from the lz4 CLI use 4 MiB blocks (measured FLG 0x64, BD 0x70 on c.lz4), so a 1 GB frame has only ~256 blocks = ~8k lanes, below the ~20k active threads where this GPU saturates (measured). Frames with dependent blocks (-BD) cannot be block-parallel at all.
candidates.granularity: Block-independent LZ4 frames (FLG bit 5 set); ideally 64 KiB blocks (lz4 -B4) giving ~16k blocks per GB; with the default 4 MiB blocks parallelism is 256 blocks per GB. Each dispatch should carry at least ~30-150 MB to amortise the 146 µs command-buffer round trip.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 10-40 GB/s on M4 Max for 64 KiB-block frames, 2-8 GB/s for 4 MiB-block frames (back-of-envelope: nvCOMP LZ4 decode reported 320 GB/s on an RTX 3090 in a search summary, unverified; scaled by measured 369 GB/s copy bandwidth vs 936 GB/s 3090 spec and by the H100 finding that short matches waste most lanes; 4 MiB-block figure limited by 256 blocks x ~10-30 MB/s per lane group).
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Apple Compression LZ4 decode measured 2.58 GB/s on one core (64 MiB, ratio 1.58 data); lz4 CLI 1.10 decode 2,847 MB/s on one core (719 MB source corpus). Multi-core bar = min(12 P-cores x ~2.7 GB/s + 4 E-cores, memory bandwidth) ≈ 25-35 GB/s (unverified; KaitoKit decodes an LZ4 frame on one thread today).
candidates.killCriterion: GPU decode of a 1 GB block-independent 64 KiB-block frame, measured commit-to-completion including zero-copy setup, below 25 GB/s, or below the 16-lane libcompression decode of the same frame in the same run.
candidates.firstExperiment: Metal kernel: one threadgroup of 32 threads per LZ4 block over a bytesNoCopy MTLBuffer of a 1 GB frame produced by 'lz4 -B4 -BI'; prefix pass on the CPU records block offsets (LZ4 block headers are 4-byte sizes, so this is a linear scan); compare output bytes to KaitoKit's decoder and time against DispatchQueue.concurrentPerform x16 of compression_decode_buffer per block.

candidates.name: Zstd frame/block decode on GPU (4 Huffman literal streams + interleaved FSE sequences + LZ sequence execution)
candidates.whatItComputes: Per zstd block (≤128 KiB): decode the Huffman-coded literals (1 or 4 streams), decode the three interleaved FSE state machines for sequences, then execute sequences (literal copies and match copies with repeat-offset history) into the output window.
candidates.mapping: Partially GPU-shaped: the 4 literal streams and 3 FSE states are independent lanes by format design, but that is 4-7-way parallelism per block, not 32; sequence execution needs a prefix-sum over literal lengths (SIMD-group friendly) and match resolution with nesting (Sitaridi MRR rounds, or serial). Huffman table max 11 bits (4 KiB x 2 B) and FSE tables ≤ 2^9 entries fit in 32 KiB threadgroup memory; the 128 KiB output block plus up to 8 MiB window do not, so copies hit device memory. nvCOMP documents zstd decompression as slower than its GDeflate. The repeat-offset history is a genuinely serial 3-entry state (2026 study: the distance history is the last sequential element).
candidates.granularity: Independent zstd frames or blocks; a 1 GB zstd -3 file has ~8k blocks of 128 KiB, enough for one threadgroup each. Batches of ≥100 MB per dispatch.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 5-15 GB/s on M4 Max (back-of-envelope: per block a threadgroup gets ~7 lanes of entropy work at the measured ~10 MB/s per lane for table-lookup loops plus vector copies; 8k blocks x ~1-2 MB/s effective per block ≈ 8-16 GB/s; nvCOMP gives no zstd number and calls its decode throughput inferior to GDeflate).
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: libzstd 1.5.7 decode measured 1,930 MB/s on one core (719 MB corpus, ratio 6.4); multi-core bar ≈ 20-25 GB/s (12 P-cores, unverified scaling). KaitoKit's own Swift ZstdDecompressor measured 197 MB/s (Documentation/verification/2026-09-12-zstd.md), ~10x slower than libzstd, a CPU gap, not a GPU opportunity.
candidates.killCriterion: A one-threadgroup-per-block GPU decoder of zstd -3 output measured below 20 GB/s on a 1 GB frame, or a CPU profile showing sequence execution (the part the GPU cannot parallelise beyond MRR) is more than half of libzstd decode time.
candidates.firstExperiment: Metal kernel that decodes only the 4-stream Huffman literals section of each block (tables built on CPU, uploaded as 4 KiB per block) and compares literal bytes with KaitoKit's ZstdHuffman output; measure GB/s of literals decoded versus libzstd full decode.

https://arxiv.org/pdf/1606.00519 (Gompresso: 256 KB blocks, 10-bit limited Huffman tables to fit on-chip memory, MRR vs DE, 2x over parallel zlib on K40)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10188 (distance history is the last genuinely sequential element; removing it costs 0.54% ratio)
https://github.com/facebook/zstd/blob/dev/README.md (zstd -1 decode 1,550 MB/s on i7-9700K, lzbench Silesia)

candidates.name: Deflate / gzip inflate on GPU (speculative or self-synchronising Huffman; GDeflate as the contrast case)
candidates.whatItComputes: Inflate of zlib/gzip/ZIP-Deflate streams: dynamic Huffman table per block, bit-serial symbol decode, LZ77 copies over a 32 KiB window; block boundaries are not byte-aligned and not indexed.
candidates.mapping: Does not map. Deflate is the worst case in every GPU library: nvCOMP calls Deflate/Gzip the slowest of its formats, Gompresso needed a modified format (limited-length codes, dependency elimination, up to 19% ratio loss) to get 2x over multi-core zlib on a K40, and Microsoft/NVIDIA created GDeflate (32 swizzled sub-streams, one lane per sub-stream) precisely because standard Deflate cannot be decoded 32-wide. Finding block starts requires speculative decoding of every bit offset (rapidgzip does this on CPUs: 5.6 GB/s on 128 cores for Silesia). Self-synchronising Huffman decoding (Weißenberger 2018) assumes one static code; Deflate changes codes per block and interleaves distance codes and extra bits, and the LZ77 window still serialises copies.
candidates.granularity: Would need a rewritten stream (GDeflate) or pre-recorded block boundaries; GyoshukuKit's gzip writer emits full-flush sync points per chunk (DeflateBlock.size chunks with a 32 KiB carried window), which gives byte-aligned entry points but each chunk still needs the previous 32 KiB window, so chunks decode in parallel only with the window handed over (the CompressedTarUpdater already does this on CPU).
candidates.expectedThroughput: 1-3 GB/s on M4 Max for standard Deflate with one threadgroup per known sync point (back-of-envelope: ~10 MB/s per serial lane, a few hundred chunks per GB); Gompresso's GPU/CPU ratio was 2x against a 2013 12-core Xeon with a modified format.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: gzip -d measured 1,591 MB/s on one core (ratio 5.2 source corpus); Compression.zlib decode 0.57 GB/s on one core on ratio-2.5 data; KaitoKit uses system zlib; multi-core bar ≈ 8-18 GB/s if chunks are known (unverified), 1.6 GB/s for an unindexed stream.
candidates.killCriterion: Already met by literature: no published GPU decoder of unmodified Deflate beats a modern multi-core zlib; the only measurable kill is a GPU inflate of GyoshukuKit sync-point chunks below the 16-lane zlib inflate of the same chunks.
candidates.firstExperiment: Do not build a GPU inflater. If a Deflate demo is wanted, implement GDeflate-style 32-sub-stream swizzling of a Deflate block on the CPU and decode it 32-wide on the GPU to show what the format would have to become; report it as an illustration, not a codec.

candidates.name: Self-synchronising / gap-array Huffman decoding on GPU (entropy stage only)
candidates.whatItComputes: Given one static canonical Huffman code and a long bitstream, every thread starts decoding at its own bit offset; because prefix codes resynchronise after a few symbols, per-thread start positions are corrected in a second pass (Weißenberger and Schmidt 2018), or the encoder records gap arrays so no correction is needed.
candidates.mapping: Maps well as a kernel: table lookups in threadgroup memory (a 12-bit table of 2-byte entries is 8 KiB, fine under 32 KiB), SIMD-group prefix sums for output positions, no atomics beyond 32-bit. Does not map to the archive formats: Deflate, LHA LH5/LH7, RAR, zstd all switch tables per block or interleave extra bits and distance codes, so synchronisation happens inside a block of tens of KB, and the measured 146 µs dispatch cost means the kernel needs ≥100 MB of same-table data per dispatch to matter.
candidates.granularity: Single-table streams of ≥100 MB; zstd literal sections (≤128 KiB) and Deflate blocks are far too small per table.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 20-60 GB/s on M4 Max for a synthetic single-table stream (back-of-envelope: paper claims >10x over zstd's Huffman decoder on TITAN V; scaled by the measured 180-200 GB/s aggregate table-lookup ceiling and the 2-pass correction).
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: zstd's Huffman decoder (HUF_decompress4X) runs at roughly 1-2 GB/s per core (unverified; the paper's CPU reference); 12 P-cores ≈ 12-24 GB/s on independent streams.
candidates.killCriterion: No format the two libraries read or write has a single-table Huffman section larger than a few hundred KB; if the demo cannot name a real input ≥100 MB per table, drop it.
candidates.firstExperiment: Only as a building block: write the kernel for zstd's 4-stream literals (see zstd candidate) and measure GB/s of literal bytes; skip the self-synchronising variant.

candidates.name: ANS / FSE decoding on GPU (multians, dietgpu, Recoil)
candidates.whatItComputes: tANS/rANS decoding with many interleaved states so each lane owns a state; dietgpu encodes with 32-way interleaving and reaches 250-410 GB/s on an A100; multians decodes an unpartitioned single-state stream via an overflow pattern.
candidates.mapping: Maps well only for streams encoded for it (interleaved states, per-warp metadata). zstd FSE uses 2-3 interleaved states over ≤128 KiB blocks, LZMA/PPMd/RAR use adaptive binary range coders whose model updates every bit, which no GPU technique parallelises. Kernel needs are modest: tables ≤ 2^12 entries in threadgroup memory, 32-bit ops, SIMD-group shuffles.
candidates.granularity: GPU-encoded ANS streams with ≥ thousands of interleaved states per dispatch; not applicable to existing archive entropy sections.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 40-100 GB/s on M4 Max for dietgpu-style streams (back-of-envelope: dietgpu 250-410 GB/s on A100 scaled by 369/1555 GB/s bandwidth ratio); zero for existing formats.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: zstd FSE/Huffman entropy stage ~1-2 GB/s per core (unverified); KaitoKit's ZstdFSE is part of the 197 MB/s Swift decoder.
candidates.killCriterion: The demo cannot produce or consume any file that KaitoKit or GyoshukuKit handle; if the owner requires interoperability with existing formats, this is dead on arrival.
candidates.firstExperiment: Skip unless a GPU-native side format is desired; then port dietgpu's ANS layout to Metal on 256 MiB of text and compare with zstd -1 entropy-only speed.
sources: https://github.com/facebookresearch/dietgpu (ANS 250-410 GB/s on A100)
https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3337821.3337888 (multians, up to 17x over 64 CPU threads and 39x over zstd's entropy codec; abstract via Semantic Scholar API)
https://github.com/weissenberger/multians (single table, radix 2, decode only, alphabet ≤256)
https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.12141 (Recoil: rANS decoding from arbitrary positions with intermediate states)

candidates.name: bzip2 block-parallel decode: one serial GPU thread (or threadgroup) per 900 kB block versus fine-grained iBWT
candidates.whatItComputes: Per bzip2 block: Huffman decode with per-50-symbol table switching, RLE2, inverse MTF, inverse BWT (a pointer-chase of block-length steps through a 3.6 MB tt array), RLE1, CRC. Blocks are independent given their bit offsets; stream starts are byte-aligned (KaitoKit Bzip2StreamLayout), block magics inside a stream are bit-aligned.
candidates.mapping: Per-block-serial mapping fails on measured numbers: one GPU thread runs a table-lookup loop at ~10 MB/s (60x slower than a P-core at 600 MB/s), an iBWT pointer chase is a dependent random access per byte, and a 1 GB archive has only ~1,200 blocks, so 1,200 x ≤10 MB/s ≤ 12 GB/s theoretical and realistically 0.2-1 GB/s once Huffman+iMTF+iBWT work per byte is counted; per-block working sets (3.6 MB tt + 256 KiB tables) kill threadgroup-memory use. The fine-grained approach (Weißenberger and Schmidt ICPP 2024) parallelises iBWT and iMTF inside a block and reached 2.4 GB/s iBWT+iMTF on an A100 and 11.6 GB/s full decode on an 8-GPU DGX H100; it needs list-ranking style passes over device memory and is bandwidth/latency bound, so it scales with the M4 Max's 369 GB/s, about 1/4 of an A100.
candidates.granularity: Concatenated bzip2 streams or blocks with known offsets; GyoshukuKit tar.bz2 writes complete streams of ≤ 5 x level x 100,000 bytes (byte-aligned starts), which KaitoKit's ParallelBzip2Decompressor already exploits with 8 workers. Batches of ≥ 500 MB per dispatch.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Per-block-serial: 0.2-1 GB/s (back-of-envelope from measured 10 MB/s per thread and 1,200 blocks per GB). Fine-grained ICPP'24 style: 0.5-1 GB/s on M4 Max (2.4 GB/s A100 iBWT+iMTF scaled by 369/1555 bandwidth; full pipeline lower).
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: libbz2 decode measured 78 MB/s on one core (ratio 7.5); KaitoKit ParallelBzip2Decompressor today: 8 workers ≈ 0.6 GB/s; libbz2 on all 12 P-cores + 4 E-cores ≈ 1.0-1.1 GB/s (unverified scaling).
candidates.killCriterion: GPU full bzip2 decode of a 1 GB tar.bz2 measured below 1.1 GB/s (16-core libbz2), or below KaitoKit's existing 8-worker path after raising its worker cap to 16, which is the cheaper fix.
candidates.firstExperiment: Port only the iBWT stage: CPU decodes to the (tt, origPtr) arrays for 1,200 blocks, GPU performs the inverse BWT with a list-ranking kernel, compare bytes and time against libbz2's iBWT share (profile libbz2 with Instruments first to know that share).

candidates.name: GPU forward BWT (suffix sorting) for bzip2 / tar.bz2 encoding
candidates.whatItComputes: Suffix-array or BWT construction of each 900 kB block (prefix-doubling radix sorts on the GPU, as libcubwt does), replacing libbz2's blocksort, then MTF/RLE/Huffman on CPU or GPU.
candidates.mapping: Sorting is the GPU's home turf: libcubwt reaches 480-640 MB/s on an RTX 4070 Ti for single 50-370 MB inputs at 20.5 bytes of GPU memory per input byte, and Apple GPUs have strong SIMD-group reductions; batching 1,000 blocks of 900 kB into one sort pass is natural. Two blockers: bandwidth (M4 Max measured 369 GB/s vs 4070 Ti 504 GB/s spec, so expect ~0.7x) and, decisively, libbz2 exposes no API to inject an external BWT (GyoshukuKit Bzip2StreamEncoder calls BZ2_bzCompressInit/BZ2_bzCompress), so the demo requires writing a bzip2 encoder (MTF, RLE2, Huffman table selection, bit packing) in Swift.
candidates.granularity: Batches of ≥ 100 bzip2 blocks (≥ 90 MB) per dispatch; GyoshukuKit's tar.bz2 chunk cutter already produces exactly these blocks.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 300-450 MB/s for the BWT stage on M4 Max (libcubwt 480-640 MB/s on 4070 Ti scaled by 369/504 bandwidth, unverified for batched small blocks); end-to-end tar.bz2 encode perhaps 250-400 MB/s if the remaining stages run on 16 CPU lanes.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: bzip2 -9 compress measured 18.6 MB/s on one core; GyoshukuKit ParallelBzip2Compressor on 12 P + 4 E cores ≈ 200-280 MB/s (unverified scaling). The BWT (blocksort) share of libbz2 compress time is unmeasured; commonly cited as the majority but unverified.
candidates.killCriterion: Either an Instruments profile of libbz2 showing blocksort below 60% of compress time (then the ceiling is < 2.5x even with a free BWT), or a batched GPU BWT of 900 kB blocks measured below 300 MB/s including the Swift encoder's remaining stages on 16 lanes.
candidates.firstExperiment: Profile BZ2_bzCompress at level 9 on a 1 GB tar with Instruments to get the blocksort share; then implement a GPU prefix-doubling suffix sort of a single 900 kB block, verify against a CPU BWT, and time 1,000 blocks batched.

candidates.name: GPU LZ77 match finding (hash-table or suffix-array) feeding LZMA2, Deflate or LH5 encoders
candidates.whatItComputes: For every input position, find the longest earlier match within the window (hash of 3-4 bytes with a bucket of recent positions, or suffix-array based LZ factorisation), producing (offset, length) candidates that a CPU parser and entropy coder consume.
candidates.mapping: The GPU part works: nvCOMP compresses LZ4 with 32 lanes reading 32 bytes and voting on matches, GPULZ reports up to 272x over prior GPU LZSS on an A4000, ACEAPEX's depth-limited encoder reaches 77 GB/s on an H100. The archive part does not: GyoshukuKit's LZMA2 encoder is Apple Compression's COMPRESSION_LZMA (LZMA2Compressor.swift), Deflate is zlib deflateInit2_, both closed to external matches; LZMA's optimal parser and adaptive range coder are serial per 16 MiB chunk regardless of who finds matches. Only LH5Encoder (8 KiB window, niche LHA) is in-house. Hash tables of 2^16-2^20 entries do not fit 32 KiB threadgroup memory, so they live in device memory with 32-bit atomics (fine, atomic_uint compiles and works).
candidates.granularity: Chunks of ≥ 16 MiB (GyoshukuKit LZMA2ChunkPipeline.chunkSize) per dispatch; deep match search (LZMA bt4 depth 32+) multiplies work 10-30x over LZ4-style greedy hashing.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 5-20 GB/s of input for LZ4-quality greedy matches on M4 Max (back-of-envelope from nvCOMP T4 >60 GB/s LZ4 compress scaled by bandwidth); 0.3-1 GB/s for LZMA-quality candidate lists (unverified); irrelevant while no encoder consumes them.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Compression.lzma encode measured 2 MB/s per core (16 MiB chunks in parallel: GyoshukuKit ParallelXZCompressor, ~30 MB/s on 16 lanes by xz -T16 analogy, measured 32 MB/s for xz -6 -T16 on 128 MiB); zlib deflate -6 80 MB/s per core (gzip CLI); Compression.lz4 encode 665 MB/s per core.
candidates.killCriterion: Already met for LZMA2 and Deflate: no encoder in either repository accepts external match candidates; the candidate revives only if the owner commits to writing an LZMA or Deflate encoder in Swift (weeks of work) whose profile shows match finding above 70% of encode time.
candidates.firstExperiment: If pursued at all, target LH5Encoder: replace its match search with a GPU pass over ≤ 1 MiB members and verify byte-identical LHA output; measure against the CPU encoder on a 1 GB LHA corpus.

candidates.name: CRC-32 / Adler-32 on GPU with parallel prefix and crc32_combine
candidates.whatItComputes: Each thread computes the CRC of a slice (table or slice-by-N in threadgroup memory), then slices are combined with the GF(2) polynomial shift (zlib crc32_combine, x^(8*len) mod P) in a SIMD-group or log-depth reduction; Adler-32 combines with modular sums.
candidates.mapping: Maps trivially, and still loses: measured on this machine, a bitwise (no-table) GPU CRC over 256 MiB runs at 84 GB/s and a table version would be bounded by the measured 369 GB/s copy bandwidth; the CPU's ARMv8 CRC instructions via zlib crc32() give 46 GB/s on one core and 243 GB/s on 16 lanes with crc32_combine (measured), with the owner's own design.md recording ~47 GB/s. Both sides are memory-bound, so the best GPU outcome is a tie, and moving data to the GPU is free only if the data is already in a bytesNoCopy MTLBuffer.

candidates.mapping: GPU T-table AES needs 4-5 KiB of tables in threadgroup memory (fits) and ~16 dependent table lookups per byte; on this GPU the measured aggregate table-lookup ceiling is ~180-200 GB/s for one lookup per byte, so AES lands around 15-30 GB/s. Published GPU AES-CTR peaks (~110 GB/s on an RTX 2070 Super) are NVIDIA numbers with bit-sliced or T-table code and much more integer throughput.

candidates.name: LZMA2 chunk-parallel decode on GPU (xz blocks, 7z LZMA2 folders)

candidates.mapping: Does not map: the range decoder is a serial chain of multiply-shift-compare-update per bit with data-dependent branches and a mutable probability model (KaitoKit LZMADecoder), the very case GPU literature never parallelises; chunks that reset state are few (a 1 GB xz has ~64 16 MiB blocks; dictionary-reset LZMA2 chunks are rarer than 2 MiB chunks, which share state), so at most ~64-500 serial GPU threads at ≤10 MB/s each; the 64 MiB dictionary per chunk is device memory only.
candidates.granularity: Only xz blocks / 7z folders that reset state; 16 MiB blocks give 64 threads per GB.
candidates.expectedThroughput: ≤ 0.1-0.6 GB/s on M4 Max (back-of-envelope: 64-500 serial lanes x ≤ 1-10 MB/s once range-coder work per byte is counted).

candidates.name: GyoshukuKit compressed-tar chunk cuts (tar.gz sync points, tar.bz2 streams, tar.xz blocks) decoded per chunk on the GPU

facts.fact: MTLDevice on this machine: maxThreadgroupMemoryLength 32,768 B, maxThreadsPerThreadgroup 1024, hasUnifiedMemory true, maxBufferLength 86.6 GB, supportsFamily(.apple9) and (.metal4) true.

Empty compute dispatch (32 threads) commit-to-waitUntilCompleted latency: median 146 µs, p10 125 µs, p90 256 µs (200 samples). To keep dispatch overhead under 10%, a dispatch must carry ≥ 1.5 ms of GPU work, e.g. ≥ 30 MB at 20 GB/s or ≥ 150 MB at 100 GB/s. This is round-trip latency, not pipelined throughput.
Simple copy kernel over 256 MiB (read + write) from a bytesNoCopy shared buffer: median 369 GB/s, max 439 GB/s by GPU timestamps; M4 Max spec is 546 GB/s.
makeBuffer(bytesNoCopy:) over posix_memalign(16384) CPU memory works with .storageModeShared (Apple silicon page size 16 KiB); malloc'd memory is not accepted, page alignment is required.

Per-thread serial decode speed on the GPU: a table-lookup CRC-style loop (1 threadgroup-memory lookup, shift, xor per byte) runs at 10.5 MB/s on 1 thread, 9.9 MB/s per thread at 40 threads, 9.6 MB/s at 5,120, 8.9 MB/s at 20,480 (181 GB/s aggregate), and aggregate saturates at ~200 GB/s from 81,920 threads. The identical loop on one CPU P-core in Swift -O runs at 600 MB/s: a 60:1 ratio per lane.

risks: Baseline scaling: the machine has 12 P-cores + 4 E-cores, not 16 equal cores, and multi-core scaling is well below 16x (xz -T16 gave ~3-4x on a 128 MiB input); every 'multi-core CPU bar' above that is not marked measured should be measured with KaitoAccelLab's baseline subcommand before the speed report quotes it.

Two different 'CPU today' numbers exist for zstd (KaitoKit Swift 197 MB/s vs libzstd 1,930 MB/s) and PPMd (14 MB/s vs 7zz ~3x faster): a GPU that beats the in-house decoder is beating a slow port, not the CPU. The report must compare against the reference library, and the cheaper win for those codecs is CPU optimisation.

Memory bandwidth is the shared ceiling: 16-lane CRC (243 GB/s) and AES (142 GB/s) already sit within 1.5-2.6x of the GPU's measured 369 GB/s, so any GPU CRC/AES result will be a tie at best and must be reported as such in advance, as plan.md already anticipates.

64-bit atomics do not compile in the runtime MSL headers on macOS 27.2 despite the feature table; kernels must be designed around 32-bit atomics (fine for hash tables and histograms, awkward for >4 GiB offsets).

Dispatch granularity: 146 µs per command buffer round trip means streaming-style codec pipelines (KaitoKit's read(into:) 256 KiB output chunks) cannot call the GPU per chunk; the GPU path needs whole-archive or ≥ 30-150 MB batches, which changes memory footprint and cancellation behaviour that the libraries carefully bound today.

Block count, not per-block speed, is the binding constraint for block-parallel decode: 1 GB of 4 MiB LZ4 blocks or 900 kB bzip2 blocks supplies 250-1,200 independent streams against a GPU that saturates near 20,000; only writer-controlled formats (GyoshukuKit could emit 64 KiB LZ4 blocks or smaller bzip2 levels) reach useful parallelism, at a ratio cost.

Encode-side offloads (GPU BWT, GPU match finding) are blocked by closed encoders (libbz2, zlib, Apple Compression LZMA) with no injection API; a demo requires writing a bzip2 or LZMA encoder in Swift, weeks of work with correctness risk, before any GPU speedup can be observed.

Literature numbers come from NVIDIA hardware with 4-9x the memory bandwidth and far larger shared memory; scaling by the 369/1555 (A100) or 369/3350 (H100) bandwidth ratio is a rough estimate and random-access stages (iBWT, hash tables) scale worse than bandwidth.

Several quoted figures are search-summary only (RTX 3090 LZ4 320 GB/s, Blackwell 42-462 GB/s, RTX 2070 Super AES 878 Gbps, Patel 2012 slowdowns); cite them as unverified or open the primary pages before the speed report.

GPU results must be byte-identical to the CPU path and verified against KaitoKit's decoders and external tools on the perf corpus; GPU kernels have no bounds checking by default, so malformed-archive hardening (a core KaitoKit property) would need explicit guards and per-dispatch validation.

Measurements here were taken on a machine that may have had background load (an xz run was killed mid-way) and without release-build harness discipline (alternating runs, noise floor) that plan.md requires; treat them as first-order anchors to be re-measured in KaitoAccelLab.

The ANE is not a candidate for any bit-manipulation codec: it executes Core ML graphs in fp16/int8 tensors, has no bit-level or table-lookup primitives, and its per-inference overhead (0.07-0.1 ms measured) suits only batched byte-prediction models for a neural-compression demo, which is a different angle from this report.

reports.summary: The Apple Neural Engine on this M4 Max (16 cores) is reachable only through Core ML model execution; no public compute API exists, and the documented private route (_ANEClient/_ANECompiler) is out of scope and fragile across OS updates. I built eight small model families with the coremltools 9.0 MIL builder (no PyTorch), read per-op placement with MLComputePlan from both Python and Swift, timed them under cpuOnly / cpuAndGPU / cpuAndNeuralEngine, and proved ANE execution with Instruments' Core AI template (ane-hw-intervals table). Core ML's planner keeps every probe on the CPU at batch <= 128 and moves matmul/conv/attention/state graphs to the ANE only at batch 1024 (threshold somewhere between 128 and 1024 for these shapes); the native `lstm` op is CPU-only per the plan, but an unrolled LSTM cell with MLState (read_state/coreml_update_state) is placed and runs on the ANE. Per call, the Core ML->ANE non-compute cost is ~157-200 us (wall minus ANE-busy at batch 1024), and a batch-1 call of any small model costs ~40 us on Core ML's CPU path because the ANE is never selected. The LSTM cell step costs 427 us at batch 1024 (0.42 us/sample) and 2.32 ms at batch 8192 (0.28 us/sample wall, 0.25 us/sample ANE-busy), i.e. an asymptote of ~4 MB/s for a 256-hidden byte model, versus 25 MB/s for 7zz PPMd decode and 141-220 MB/s for LZMA2 decode on the same corpus and machine; the ANE beats Core ML's own CPU path by only 1.2-1.7x. Outputs are not bit-identical between ANE and CPU (fp16 datapath; softmax rows sum to ~0.9994), so any ANE-decoded archive is tied to the ANE path. Recommendation: build the neural byte-predictor demo (candidate 1) only as a compression-ratio demonstration with the kill criterion below; the first experiment is already reproducible from the scratchpad harness (models/lstmstate_1024.mlmodelc + ane_bench + xctrace). Do not pursue non-ML uses of the ANE (CRC, Huffman, LZ matching, AES): the datapath is fp16-only with no integer, gather/scatter/one_hot or data-dependent control flow.

candidates.name: Batched LSTM byte predictor + arithmetic coding (NNCP/DeepZip style)
candidates.whatItComputes: For N independent blocks in parallel, one recurrent step per byte position: p(byte_t | h_{t-1}) as a 256-way softmax from an LSTM cell (here 256 input, 256 hidden, 256 out; 0.66 M params); h and c are kept in MLState across calls; the CPU turns each probability row into an integer frequency table and drives a range/arithmetic coder. Compression and decompression are symmetric: both step the recurrence once per byte per block (teacher forcing does not remove the h_{t-1} dependence).
candidates.mapping: Fits the ANE's shape: matmul + sigmoid/tanh + elementwise on [B,256] fp16 tensors, all reported supported=[CPU, NeuralEngine] by MLComputePlan, and MLState read/write ops were placed on the ANE and executed there (xctrace: 212 ane-hw-intervals labelled lstmstate_1024_main__Op0_AneInference). Does not fit the ANE's economics: per-call non-compute cost ~200 us (wall 427 us vs ANE-busy 225 us at B=1024) and the ANE-busy asymptote is 0.25 us/sample (B=8192), so the engine delivers ~5 TFLOP/s effective on this cell, and only 1.17-1.27x over Core ML's CPU path. The native MIL `lstm` op is supported=[CPU] only and never reaches the ANE; the cell must be written unrolled. Precision: fp16 datapath; softmax rows sum to 0.9994 on ANE and digests differ from cpuOnly, so encoder and decoder must run on the same compute unit and re-quantize on CPU.
candidates.granularity: Input split into >= 1024 independent blocks processed in lockstep (batch is baked into the MLState shape at conversion; last partial batch needs padding or a second model). Blocks of >= 64 KiB give 64 MiB minimum per archive to fill the batch; smaller inputs run below the planner threshold and land on the CPU (all probes at B <= 128 were planned CPU). candidates.name: Transformer byte predictor with MLState KV cache
candidates.whatItComputes: Same coding scheme as candidate 1 but the predictor is a small decoder-only transformer; MLState holds the per-block K/V cache (slice_update into a fixed max-context buffer) so decode is one token step per call; compression can run a whole block through one causal pass (position-parallel), unlike the LSTM.
candidates.mapping: layer_norm, matmul, scaled_dot_product_attention, add, slice, squeeze, softmax were all planned NeuralEngine at B=1024 under cpuAndNeuralEngine (attn_1024) and GPU under .all, so the graph maps; Apple's own guidance is (B,C,1,S) layout, per-head chunking, and no reshape/transpose to avoid memory copies. The paper measures the GPU overtaking the ANE on a self-attention block near batch 6 and on an encoder block near batch 23 (M1), so for B=1024 blocks the ANE is not the throughput winner on attention-heavy graphs. Decode still pays the ~160-200 us Core ML->ANE per-call cost; the measured full-recompute S=32, d=128 single layer costs 2.05 ms at B=1024 (2.0 us/sample), and a KV-cached step would sit between the LSTM cell (0.42 us/sample) and that number.
candidates.granularity: Same >= 1024 independent blocks; context window fixed at conversion (state buffer of B x heads x max_len x d fp16, e.g. 1024 x 4 x 1024 x 32 x 2 B = 256 MiB per layer for 1024-token context); block length must not exceed max_len.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Back-of-envelope from measurements: decode >= 200 us overhead + ANE compute per step; with the S=32 full-recompute layer measured at 2.05 ms/step (B=1024) => 0.5 MB/s; with KV cache and 2-4 layers of d=128 expect roughly 0.6-1.5 ms/step => 0.7-1.7 MB/s decode. Compression one-pass could be 5-20x faster than decode. Ratio: NNCP-class ratios (1.19 bpb enwik8) require ~100 M-parameter models at 240 us/byte on CPU (LTCB nncp v3.2: 241,871 ns/byte); a model that fits our latency budget will be far from that.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Same as candidate 1: 7zz PPMd o6 25 MB/s decode at ratio 5.25 on the corpus; LZMA2 141-220 MB/s decode.
candidates.killCriterion: If a KV-cached decode step at B=1024 measures > 0.5 ms wall on the ANE (i.e. < 2 MB/s) while the model does not beat PPMd's ratio on the perf corpus, drop it in favour of candidate 1 or nothing. Also kill if MLComputePlan shows attention ops preferred GPU/CPU under cpuAndNeuralEngine for the KV-cached shapes.

facts.fact: The ANE is reachable by applications only through Core ML model execution; there is no public compute API. A private route (_ANEClient/_ANECompiler, callable from user space) exists but is undocumented, unsupported and fragile across OS updates, and is out of scope here.
MLComputeDevice.allComputeDevices on this machine reports ANE with totalCoreCount 16, GPU and CPU (macOS 27.2, Apple M4 Max).
MLComputeUnits raw values: cpuOnly=0, cpuAndGPU=1, all=2, cpuAndNeuralEngine=3; cpuAndNeuralEngine is available from macOS 13.0 / iOS 16.0. There is no ANE-only option.

With .all, Core ML planned the batch-1024 attention model on the GPU; with .cpuAndNeuralEngine the same model was planned and ran on the ANE. Preferring the ANE therefore means MLModelConfiguration.computeUnits = .cpuAndNeuralEngine, with the CPU as the only fallback.

MLComputePlan (macOS 14.4+ / iOS 17.4+) exposes per-op placement statically: Swift `MLComputePlan.load(contentsOf:configuration:)`, `.modelStructure` -> `.program(...)`, `functions["main"].block.operations`, `plan.deviceUsage(for: op)` -> `.preferred` / `.supported`, `plan.estimatedCost(of: op)?.weight`; Python `ct.models.compute_plan.MLComputePlan.load_from_path(path, compute_units)`, `get_compute_device_usage_for_mlprogram_operation`, `get_estimated_cost_for_mlprogram_operation`. Both readers agreed on all 18 first-wave models. It must be given a compiled .mlmodelc (ct.models.utils.compile_model); an .mlpackage path aborts the process (SIGABRT), so run it in a subprocess.

facts.fact: Core ML's planner kept every probe on the CPU at batch 1, 16 and 128 (including a 256->2048->256 MLP), and preferred the ANE for matmul/conv/attention/state graphs at batch 1024, 4096 and 8192. The threshold for these shapes lies between 128 and 1024 and is not a simple MAC-count rule.

Ops reported supported=[CPU, NeuralEngine] by MLComputePlan on this machine: matmul, conv, relu, softmax, sigmoid, tanh, add, mul, split, layer_norm, scaled_dot_product_attention, slice_by_index, squeeze, read_state, write_state. The MIL `lstm` op is reported supported=[CPU] only.

Independent of Core ML, compile-and-run probes show recurrent gru/lstm/rnn cells, reduce_prod, scatter family, one_hot, non_zero, shape, band_part, mod, logical and/or/xor have no ANE path on any family M1-M5; gather runs only in a tiny software envelope; top-k, sort and dynamic-slice are rejected by the code generator (M1); control flow must be static (no data-dependent branching or loop counts); tensors are rank <= 5 with each axis <= 16384; matmul requires depth 1.

The ANE datapath is fp16 (wide accumulator only); fp32/int32/bf16 annotations are accepted by the frontend but never execute on the engine; program inputs are fp16 or uint8 (for in-graph dequantization). Apple's own article states the ANE operates in float16.

int8: A17 Pro / M4 have an int8-int8 ANE compute path; coremltools recommends W8A8 activation quantization only when the model runs mostly on the ANE (CPU/GPU slow down); Anemll measured 1.88x FP16->W8A8 throughput on M5/A18 Pro with coremltools >= 9.0 (quantize/dequantize + constexpr_affine_dequantize). Not measured in this session.

Per-call cost through Core ML to the ANE on this machine: mlp_1024 wall median 203.5 us vs ANE-busy 46.9 us (~157 us non-compute); lstmstate_1024 wall 427.0 us vs ANE-busy 225.2 us (~200 us). These include ~1 MiB of input/output copy and state I/O, so they are upper bounds on the dispatch floor, which could not be isolated because the planner refuses to send a trivial model to the ANE.

Literature dispatch floor: on M1 a tiny conv+relu+mean graph costs ~190 us per call, ~98% software/firmware overhead (25 us binding + 16 us request build + 130 us firmware round trip + 10 us completion); the roofline states a 0.23 ms floor under any single dispatch; the driver keeps one command in flight (two threads serialize at 1.04x); fusing 32 layers keeps per-call latency flat at ~0.19 ms and batching to 512 samples cuts per-sample cost from ~196 us to ~1.5 us.

A batch-1 prediction of any of these small models costs ~32-45 us wall on Core ML and runs on the CPU regardless of computeUnits, because the planner never selects the ANE for them; floor_1024 (conv1x1 + relu) produced 0 ANE hardware intervals under Instruments.

LSTM cell step (256 in, 256 hidden, 256-way softmax, MLState h/c) wall median: 39.7 us at B=1 (CPU), 55.1 us at 16 (CPU), 128.4 us at 128 (CPU), 427.0 us at 1024 (ANE, 0.417 us/sample), 1293 us at 4096 (ANE, 0.316 us/sample), 2323 us at 8192 (ANE, 0.284 us/sample); ANE-busy 225 us at 1024 and 2053 us at 8192 (0.25 us/sample asymptote => ~4 MB/s). cpuOnly at 8192: 2947 us (0.36 us/sample).

Small transformer step (one layer, d=128, S=32 full recompute, 256-way softmax) at B=1024: 2053 us on ANE (2.0 us/sample), 2387 us on cpuAndGPU (first call 609 ms shader compile); cpuOnly crashed with SIGSEGV (exit 139), reproduced twice, cause not investigated. At B=1 it costs ~40 us on the CPU.

MLState (macOS 15+ / iOS 18+) works with ANE placement: read_state/write_state ops were preferred NeuralEngine at B >= 1024 and the whole graph ran as one ANE program (Instruments label lstmstate_1024_main__Op0_AneInference). The batch size is baked into the state shape at conversion; predictions sharing one MLState must be serialized; state must not be read or written while a prediction is in flight.

Outputs are not bit-identical across compute units: at B=1024 the softmax digests differ between cpuAndNeuralEngine and cpuOnly (mlp 1023.365 vs 1023.996; lstmstate 1023.337 vs 1024.003; attn 1023.383 vs 1024.001 for 1024 rows that should each sum to 1), i.e. fp16 rows sum to ~0.9994 on the ANE. At B <= 128 digests were identical only because both settings ran on the CPU.

Batch-position invariance (a row computed alone equals the same row inside a batch) was not tested here; the only evidence is the paper's M1 direct-path measurement that row zero is invariant across batch sizes 1-128.

coremltools 9.0 builds Core ML models without PyTorch: `from coremltools.converters.mil import Builder as mb`; `@mb.program(input_specs=[mb.TensorSpec(shape, dtype=types.fp16), mb.StateTensorSpec(shape, dtype=types.fp16)], opset_version=ct.target.macOS15)`; numpy fp16 constants passed directly to mb.matmul/mb.conv; `mb.read_state`, `mb.coreml_update_state`, `mb.lstm`, `mb.scaled_dot_product_attention`, `mb.layer_norm`; `ct.convert(prog, convert_to="mlprogram", minimum_deployment_target=ct.target.macOS15, compute_precision=ct.precision.FLOAT16, skip_model_load=True)`; `model.save(path.mlpackage)`; `ct.models.utils.compile_model(pkg, destination_path=...)` -> .mlmodelc. The older neural_network builder is not needed and does not support mlprogram/state.

MIL-builder gotcha: the value returned by mb.coreml_update_state must be what downstream ops consume, and the update must be emitted in program order; otherwise coremltools 9.0's optimize_state pass raises KeyError during ct.convert.

facts.fact: Layout matters: putting the batch on N with singleton H,W ([B,256,1,1]) took 5.7 ms on the ANE at B=1024 versus 0.36-1.7 ms on the CPU, while the same MLP as [B,256] matmul took 203 us and as [1,256,1,1024] conv1x1 took 240 us. Apple's rule is (B,C,1,S) with the long axis last.

Core ML's GPU path was the slowest for every model where it engaged (mlpbig_1024: 1252 us GPU vs 317 us ANE vs 525 us CPU) with 100-600 ms first-call shader compilation; reaching the GPU through Core ML is not a substitute for Metal.

GPU vs ANE crossover (M1, direct path): GPU overtakes the ANE on throughput near batch 23 for an encoder block and near batch 6 for a self-attention block; the ANE saturates near batch 1 on those; vision convolution stays 3.6-5.7x faster on the ANE at every batch; energy crossover on large matmul near batch 16.

CPU codec baseline on this machine, 11,395,195 B text corpus, median of 3: 7zz PPMd o6 mem64m mt1 compress 28.1 / decompress 25.3 MB/s, ratio 5.25; 7zz LZMA2 mx9 mt1 4.6 / 220 MB/s, ratio 5.16; xz -9 -T1 4.2 / 141 MB/s; gzip -6 55.1 / 742 MB/s, ratio 3.62; bzip2 -9 24.9 / 64 MB/s, ratio 4.80; zstd -19 4.3 / 699 MB/s, ratio 5.07; zstd -3 187 / 606 MB/s. These are reference tools, not KaitoKit/GyoshukuKit numbers.

KaitoKit and GyoshukuKit have no recorded MB/s figures in their Documentation, verification notes or memory; the harnesses to obtain them are `kaito bench <archive> [reps] [--data|--random]` (KaitoKit/Sources/kaito/Commands/Bench.swift) and GyoshukuKit/Benchmarks/run.sh (gyoshuku-bench zip|tgz|tbz|txz|7z|lha with --references for zip/xz/7zz).

Neural compressor ratios: NNCP (transformer) 1.19 bpb on enwik8 vs cmix 1.19, xz 1.99, gzip 2.92; on LTCB nncp v3.2 compresses at 241,871 ns/byte and decompresses at 238,670 ns/byte (~4 KB/s) with 7.6 GB RAM, versus 7zip (LZMA/PPMd) 503 / 546 ns/byte and zstd -22 decompress 2.2 ns/byte on older hardware.

Apple's ANE transformer guidance: use (B,C,1,S) channels-first 4D tensors (swap nn.Linear for 1x1 conv), chunk per head, avoid reshape/transpose (memory copies), and expect bandwidth-boundness (latency roughly constant across sequence lengths 32-128); distilbert seq 128 batch 1 measured 3.47 ms at 0.454 W on iPhone 13.

risks: Speed verdict is already negative: the best measured ANE path (LSTM cell) tops out at ~3.5 MB/s wall / ~4 MB/s ANE-busy asymptote against 25 MB/s PPMd and 141-220 MB/s LZMA2 decode on the same machine; the ANE beats Core ML's own CPU path by only 1.2-1.7x. Any ANE demo is a ratio demo, not a speed demo, and the report should say so before the numbers.

Cross-compute-unit determinism is absent (fp16 datapath; digests differ between ANE and CPU at B=1024). Encoder and decoder must run the same model on the same compute unit and OS; an OS/ANE-compiler update can change fp16 results and make existing archives undecodable. Batch-position invariance on the Core ML path is unverified here and must be tested before any format decision.

Placement is not under application control: Core ML's planner chose the CPU for every probe at batch <= 128 and there is no ANE-only mode. A decoder that relies on ANE speed silently degrades to the CPU path for small inputs or after an OS update; with .cpuAndNeuralEngine the CPU is the only fallback, and attn_1024 on cpuOnly crashed (SIGSEGV) in this session, so a fallback can crash rather than slow down.

The measured ~157-200 us per-call non-compute cost includes I/O copies and could not be isolated as a pure dispatch floor because the planner refuses trivial models; treat it as an upper bound consistent with the paper's 0.19-0.23 ms (M1). Per-call overhead is amortized only by batch >= 1024 blocks, which forces >= 64 MiB inputs at 64 KiB blocks and a fixed batch baked into the MLState shape (padding or a second model for the tail).

Compression ratio of a model small enough for this latency budget is unverified; NNCP-class ratios come from ~100 M-parameter transformers at 240 us/byte on CPU. If a <= 1 M-parameter model does not beat PPMd o6 on the perf corpus, candidate 1 has no remaining justification.
int8 (W8A8) on the M4 ANE was not measured; it halves compute and I/O bytes, neither of which was the binding constraint (per-call overhead and recurrence were).

CPU baselines quoted are reference CLIs (xz, 7zz, gzip, zstd, bzip2) on a 11.4 MB text corpus, not KaitoKit/GyoshukuKit code; the repositories have no recorded MB/s. Measure with `kaito bench` and `Benchmarks/run.sh` on the perf corpus before writing the speed report. The corpus is source code, which compresses unusually well (ratio ~5); binaries/media will differ.

Tooling risks: the owner's Python 3.14 venv cannot run predictions or MLComputePlan (no libcoremlpython); MLComputePlan.load_from_path aborts the process on an .mlpackage path; ANE outputs have padded strides that naive Swift readers misinterpret; coremltools' optimize_state pass fails unless coreml_update_state outputs are consumed in program order.

Measurements were taken with other user processes present (single session, medians of 40-300 calls after 10 warmups); p90 exceeded the median by up to 30% on CPU paths. Repeat under the plan's alternating, noise-floor protocol before publishing numbers.

The Bryngelson paper's numbers are for M1 (and M5) via the private path; its M4 rows are decompile-derived, not measured. Use it for qualitative op support and the shape of the roofline, and this session's numbers for M4 Max magnitudes.

reports.summary: Neural lossless compression is a probability model driving an arithmetic/range coder; encoder and decoder run the identical model in lock step, one byte per step per stream, so the only parallelism is across many independent blocks batched into one inference. Prior art spans cmix v21 (enwik8 14.6%, ~1.6 KB/s, 31 GB RAM) and NNCP v3.2 (enwik8 14.9%, ~4.2 KB/s on a Ryzen 9 3900 + RTX 4090) at the ratio extreme, through TRACE/DZip online-trained models at 7-20 KB/s on a GPU, to L3TC (2024), which ran 200K-3.2M-parameter RWKV byte models on an iPhone 12 Neural Engine through Core ML at batch 256 and reached 376 KB/s character-level (1.30 MB/s only with a 3.29-byte/token tokenizer) at enwik9 ratios of 16-18%, versus xz/LZMA2 at 23-25% and PPMd at 21.9%. I measured on this M4 Max: a 788K-parameter GRU-cell byte predictor built with the coremltools MIL builder (no LSTM op, state as tensors, one fixed-shape model per batch) runs every op on the ANE (MLComputePlan) with a per-step latency L of 0.25 ms at B=256, 0.7 ms at B=1024 and 2.2 ms at B=4096, i.e. 1.0, 1.45 and 1.86 MB/s byte-level (formula bytes/s = B*G/L, G = bytes per step = 1); a 2.95M-parameter model gives 0.9-0.95 MB/s at B=4096. ANE output is bitwise repeatable and batch-shape invariant, but differs from the CPU path by up to 3e-3 in logits, so encoder and decoder must use the same compute unit and model file. The Core ML CPU_ONLY path of the same model reaches 1.0 MB/s at B=4096 using only ~1.7 threads, so the ANE's speed advantage is 1.5-1.8x over that path and a deliberately 12-thread CPU implementation (untested) might close or reverse it; the defensible NPU value is offload (CPU ~80% idle during ANE steps) plus a modest speedup. Against measured enwik8 baselines (zstd -19 26.94% at 2.4 MB/s encode / ~830 MB/s decode; xz -9 24.87% at 1.68 MB/s encode / 128 MB/s decode; 7-Zip PPMd o32 21.92% at 5.8 MB/s both ways), a trained 0.8-3M model should cut Wikipedia-like text to roughly 16-18% (from sources; must be re-measured with the fp16 Core ML model) at ~0.9-1.9 MB/s symmetric, which is faster than xz -9 encoding but ~100x slower than its decoding, and it will lose badly on non-text data unless gated to a CPU codec. Recommended first step: a Swift harness that loads the B=1024/4096 .mlpackage, drives a 32-bit range coder with 15-bit quantised CDFs over 2048-byte blocks on enwik8 with random weights to prove lock-step round-trip and end-to-end bytes/s, then train the 0.8M and 3M RWKV/GRU models on enwik8 with PyTorch-MPS in the existing venv (hours, not days) and verify the ratio on held-out enwik9 slices against PPMd's 21.92%.

candidates.name: Recurrent byte predictor (GRU/RWKV cell as matmul+elementwise) on ANE + CPU range coder
candidates.whatItComputes: For each of B independent blocks, one step per byte: new hidden state and a 256-way probability distribution for the next byte; the CPU quantises each distribution to a 15-bit integer CDF and range-codes the actual byte (encoder) or decodes it (decoder). Both sides run the identical fp16 Core ML model in lock step.
candidates.mapping: Fits: the step is B parallel small matmuls (256-512 wide) plus sigmoid/tanh/mul/add, all ANE-supported ops; MLComputePlan placed every op (linear/conv, concat, sigmoid, tanh, mul, add, sub, cast) on MLNeuralEngineComputeDevice for B>=256 in both [B,C] linear and [1,C,1,B] conv layouts (conv layout was ~5% faster). Recurrent state passes as input/output tensors now, MLState later (macOS 15+). Weights fp16 (1.6 MB for 788K params, 5.9 MB for 2.95M). Does not fit at small B: Core ML runs B=1 on the CPU regardless of compute unit (0.058 ms/step = 17 KB/s), and the per-call floor is 0.03-0.05 ms. Utilisation is low: 2*params*B/L gives ~2.9 TFLOPS (788K model) and ~5.6 TFLOPS (2.95M model) at B=4096 versus a claimed 38 TOPS peak, so wider layers cost little extra latency (wider-not-deeper). Numerics: ANE output is bitwise repeatable and identical for the same rows at B=256/1024/4096, but differs from CPU_ONLY by up to 1.8e-3 (small) / 3.2e-3 (large) in logits and from GPU by up to 1.3e-3, so encoder and decoder must use the same compute unit; the probability->integer CDF step must be integer-deterministic. Byte-level G=1 is the apples-to-apples figure; L3TC's 1.30 MB/s was 256 blocks x 3.29 bytes/token with a 16K tokenizer, and their character-level RWKV-200K was 376 KB/s (batch 128) on an iPhone 12; byte-grouping/tokenisation multiplies speed by G at a ratio cost and Delétang Table 2 shows BPE hurts sub-1M models.
candidates.granularity: Blocks of 2048 bytes (training sequence length; the recurrent state carries so 8-64 KiB blocks are possible, trading parallelism for ratio), B blocks per step, fixed shapes: one compiled model per B in {256, 1024, 4096}, last batch padded. Rated speed needs input >= B x block size: 8 MiB for B=4096 at 2 KiB blocks, 2 MiB for B=1024, 512 KiB for B=256; below that fall back to the CPU codec. A 100 KB file gives B=50, roughly 20x below headline.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Formula: bytes/s = B*G / (L(B) + t_coder(B) - overlap), ~ B*G / max(L, t_coder) with two half-batches pipelined between ANE and CPU. Measured L (Python predict(), median of 20, warm; Swift MLModel.prediction should be lower): 788K model: B=256 0.24-0.26 ms -> 1.0-1.06 MB/s; B=1024 0.69-0.72 ms -> 1.43-1.49 MB/s; B=4096 2.18-2.23 ms -> 1.84-1.88 MB/s; B=16384 8.2 ms -> 2.0 MB/s. 2.95M model: B=256 0.35-0.44 ms -> 0.59-0.73 MB/s; B=1024 1.12-1.21 ms -> 0.85-0.91 MB/s; B=4096 4.3-4.6 ms -> 0.90-0.95 MB/s. Range coding 4096 symbols with a 256-entry CDF costs ~0.2-0.3 ms on one core (back-of-envelope, ~50-70 ns/symbol) and hides under L with 2+ cores. Ratio expectation (from sources, trained models of this size on enwik9, not measured here): 0.8M-class 17.6% (L3TC-800K) to 21.7% (Delétang Transformer 800K); 3.2M-class 16.2% (L3TC) to 17.0% raw / 17.7% adjusted (Delétang). CPU stays ~80% idle during ANE steps (cpu_time/wall 0.21-0.39).
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Ratio: 7-Zip PPMd o=32 mem=1g (KaitoKit decodes PPMd, GyoshukuKit does not write it) measured 21.92% on enwik8 at 5.8 MB/s encode / 5.5 MB/s decode single-threaded; xz -9 24.87% at 1.68 MB/s encode / 128 MB/s decode; zstd -19 26.94% at 2.43 MB/s (1 thread; 6.5 MB/s with -T0) / ~830 MB/s decode. Same-model CPU path: Core ML CPU_ONLY (BNNS) 788K model B=4096 3.9 ms -> 1.02 MB/s using only ~1.7 threads; 2.95M model 6.6-6.8 ms -> 0.6 MB/s using ~4.6 threads. A deliberately 12-thread block-parallel CPU implementation was not measured and could reach several MB/s.
candidates.killCriterion: Either (a) a 12-thread CPU run of the same fp16 model (blocks split across P-cores, BNNS/Accelerate) reaches >= the ANE's bytes/s at the same B, so the NPU adds offload only; or (b) a <= 3M-parameter model trained <= 4 GPU-hours on enwik8 does not beat PPMd's 21.92% on a held-out enwik9 slice (e.g. bytes 100M-200M) when coded through the fp16 Core ML model; or (c) end-to-end Swift round-trip with the range coder falls below 500 KB/s at B=4096.
candidates.firstExperiment: Swift harness in KaitoAccelLab: load models/gru_conv_B1024_E128_H256.mlpackage (random weights, already converted), feed fp16 MLMultiArray one-hot + state, confirm MLComputePlan placement and step latency in Swift; add a 32-bit range coder with 15-bit CDFs (freq_i = max(1, round(p_i*(2^15-256)))+1) and round-trip 8 MiB of enwik8 through 2048-byte blocks at B=1024 and 4096, checking byte-identical output and end-to-end MB/s. Ratio ~100% is expected with random weights; the experiment proves lock-step correctness and the speed formula. Then train E128/H256 and E256/H512 RWKV/GRU byte models with PyTorch 2.14 MPS on enwik8 (20 epochs, seq 2048, batch 64, AdamW as in L3TC), export via coremltools 9 or the MIL builder, and measure enwik9[100M:200M] ratio.

candidates.name: Same recurrent byte predictor on the GPU (Core ML CPU_AND_GPU path; MPSGraph/Metal kernel as the real target)
candidates.whatItComputes: Identical per-step computation to the ANE candidate (B parallel GRU/RWKV cells producing 256-way distributions), executed on the 40-core GPU; range coding stays on the CPU.
candidates.mapping: Fits in shape: B independent rows are a natural threadgroup-per-block mapping and the weights (1.6-6 MB fp16) fit in unified memory with no copies. Measured through Core ML's GPU path (a lower bound for a hand-written kernel): 788K model B=256 0.81 ms (0.32 MB/s), B=1024 1.6 ms (0.64 MB/s), B=4096 4.2-4.5 ms (0.9-0.98 MB/s), B=16384 6.8 ms (2.4 MB/s, the only point where GPU beat ANE's 2.0 MB/s); 2.95M model B=4096 4.8-5.6 ms (0.73-0.85 MB/s). Per-step dispatch overhead dominates at small B; a hand MPSGraph/Metal loop with a persistent command buffer and fp16 simdgroup matmuls could cut it (not measured). Numerics: GPU conv-layout output was NOT batch-shape invariant (9.8e-4 difference for the same rows at B=256 vs 1024), so a GPU decoder must use exactly the encoder's B and padding.
candidates.granularity: Same block/batch structure as the ANE candidate; the GPU needs B >= 16384 blocks (>= 32 MiB of input at 2 KiB blocks) before it beats the ANE via Core ML.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 0.9-1.0 MB/s at B=4096 and 2.4 MB/s at B=16384 for the 788K model via Core ML (measured); L3TC's RWKV-200K at batch 2048 reached 1.32 MB/s character-level-equivalent on an A100 (4.35 MB/s with the 3.29-byte tokenizer), suggesting a well-written kernel on M4 Max might land at 2-5 MB/s (unverified back-of-envelope).
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Same as ANE candidate (PPMd 21.92% at 5.8 MB/s; Core ML CPU path 1.0 MB/s at B=4096 on ~1.7 threads), plus the ANE path itself (1.86 MB/s at B=4096, 2.0 MB/s at B=16384).
candidates.killCriterion: A hand MPSGraph/Metal implementation of the per-step cell does not beat the ANE's bytes/s at B <= 4096 (the B the typical input granularity permits); Core ML's GPU path already loses to the ANE at every B <= 4096.
candidates.firstExperiment: Reuse the Swift harness with computeUnits = .cpuAndGPU and record L(B) for B in {1024, 4096, 16384}; if promising, write an MPSGraph version of the GRU step with fp16 weights resident and one command buffer per step, and compare L.

candidates.name: Transformer / attention byte predictor on ANE (Delétang-style small transformer, TRACE-style single layer)
candidates.whatItComputes: Per byte, attention over the block's previous bytes (KV cache in MLState) plus an FFN, producing the next-byte distribution; decode is one step per byte with a growing cache.
candidates.mapping: Matmuls and softmax are ANE ops, but per-step decode needs attention over up to 2048 cached positions per block per byte (O(context) work per byte) and a KV cache of B x layers x 2 x 2048 x d fp16 (for B=1024, d=128, 2 layers: 2 GiB), and stateful KV-cache models are a recent Core ML feature (macOS 15) whose ANE placement is unproven here. L3TC measured Transformer-200K at 15 KB/s and Transformer-XL-200K at 29 KB/s on the iPhone 12 ANE at batch 256 versus 750 KB/s for RWKV-200K (same platform, tokenised), i.e. 25-50x slower than the recurrent model at equal size; TRACE's single-layer transformer needed online back-propagation on an RTX 2080Ti to reach ~16-20 KB/s. Ratios at equal parameter count are similar or worse than RWKV (Delétang Transformer 3.2M 17.0% vs L3TC-3.2M 16.2% on enwik9).
candidates.granularity: Same 2048-byte blocks and B-way batching; additionally needs a per-block KV cache resident across 2048 steps.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Expected 20-100 KB/s byte-level at B=1024 on this ANE (back-of-envelope from L3TC's 15-29 KB/s on an A14-class ANE scaled by the ~1.4x step-latency ratio observed here), i.e. an order of magnitude below the recurrent model.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: PPMd 21.92% at 5.8 MB/s; the recurrent ANE model at 1.45-1.86 MB/s.
candidates.killCriterion: Per-step latency with KV cache at B=1024 exceeds 5 ms (< 200 KB/s), or MLComputePlan shows the attention/gather ops off the ANE. Expected to be killed; include only to document why recurrent wins.
candidates.firstExperiment: Build a 2-layer d=64 causal transformer step model with MLState KV cache in the MIL builder, B=1024, and time one step at cache length 1024 under CPU_AND_NE with MLComputePlan placement.

candidates.name: cmix / paq8 class context mixing with a neural mixer (CPU state of the art)
candidates.whatItComputes: Per bit: hundreds of context-model predictions looked up in large hash tables, mixed by small gated linear/neural mixers (cmix adds an LSTM byte model), followed by SSE stages and a binary arithmetic coder; the model adapts online on every bit.
candidates.mapping: Does not map: the work per bit is dominated by dependent random-access hash-table lookups (cmix v21 uses ~31 GB) and tiny per-bit updates, with no batch dimension inside one stream; there is no independent-block structure without discarding the adaptive state that gives it its ratio, and the ANE cannot execute the table lookups or the online weight updates. Speeds: cmix v21 622,949 ns/byte compress (~1.6 KB/s), NNCP v3.2 241,871 ns/byte (~4.1 KB/s; Bellard's readme: enwik9 in 2.8 days on a Ryzen 9 3900 + RTX 4090, GPU memory 6.6 GB).
candidates.granularity: Whole stream, single-threaded per stream; parallelism only across separate files/streams on CPU cores.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 1.6-4 KB/s (from LTCB), 200-500x slower than the recurrent ANE model; ratios enwik8 14.6% (cmix v21) / 14.9% (nncp v3.2), enwik9 10.8% / 10.7%.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: It is the CPU ceiling for ratio; KaitoKit's PPMd (order-32, 21.9% on enwik8 at ~6 MB/s) is the practical CPU context-model baseline.
candidates.killCriterion: By construction: no per-bit accelerator dispatch below ~0.03 ms exists (measured floor), so even an ideal ANE per-bit call would cap at ~4 KB/s. Not worth pursuing on GPU/ANE.
candidates.firstExperiment: None; document as the ratio reference point in the explanatory document.

candidates.whatItComputes: A large pretrained language model (LLaMA-7B, Chinchilla 70B, or tszip's text-only transformer) supplies next-token probabilities to an arithmetic coder over tokenised text.
candidates.mapping: Ratios are unmatched (Chinchilla 70B 8.3% raw on enwik9, Llama 2 7B 8.9%, LLMZip 0.71 bits/char on text8) but the model is 13-140 GB and the throughput is 280 B/s (Llama2-7B) and 85 B/s (Llama2-13B) on an A100 at batch 2048; adjusted for model size the rate is >1400% on 1 GB. tszip runs at 180 KB/s on an A100 with 13.83% on enwik8 but 351.83% adjusted. candidates.granularity: Text only, tokenised, 2048-token windows.
candidates.expectedThroughput: < 1 KB/s for 7B-class models (from L3TC Table 4); tszip-class 100-200 KB/s on a data-centre GPU, likely tens of KB/s here (unverified).
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Not applicable; ratio only.
candidates.killCriterion: Already killed by the source numbers (280 B/s, model >> data); include for the explanatory document only.

candidates.name: DZip / TRACE-style train-on-the-input (online-adapted small model)
candidates.whatItComputes: A small RNN/transformer trained (DZip: bootstrap pass, weights stored in the archive; TRACE/NNCP: online back-propagation during coding) on the very stream being compressed, so no distribution mismatch, followed by arithmetic coding.
candidates.mapping: Training requires back-propagation, which Core ML on the ANE does not offer for mlprogram models; it maps only to the GPU (Metal/MPSGraph or PyTorch-MPS). Reported speeds are low: DZip README 'approximately 5 hours/MB' (Keras), TRACE Table 2 on an RTX 2080Ti: Dzip ~399 KB/min (~6.7 KB/s), TRACE ~952 KB/min, TRACE+BP controller ~1229 KB/min (~20 KB/s) with batch 512 and 2.4M parameters (± signs lost in extraction; TRACE's text asserts ~2-3x over Dzip). The GPU time is dominated by the backward pass, so the ANE brings nothing.
candidates.granularity: Whole file or large corpus (>= 100 MB) so that model-weight overhead and training time amortise; TRACE used byte groups of 4 and context 8.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 10-30 KB/s on this GPU (back-of-envelope from TRACE's 2080Ti numbers; unverified), 50-100x slower than the fixed pretrained ANE model.
candidates.killCriterion: Measured training+coding throughput on the GPU below 100 KB/s, or ratio not better than the fixed pretrained model on the same data; only revisit if the corpus is multi-GB and hours are acceptable.
candidates.firstExperiment: None before the fixed-model demo exists; if pursued, time one training step of the 788K model at batch 512 x seq 2048 in PyTorch-MPS.

candidates.name: Same recurrent model on the CPU via BNNS/Accelerate (AMX), block-parallel across P-cores
candidates.whatItComputes: Identical per-step GRU/RWKV computation, executed with Accelerate/BNNS fp16 matmuls (which use the AMX units) with the B blocks split across 12 P-core threads; the range coder runs in the same threads.
candidates.mapping: Core ML's CPU_ONLY path already does this partially: 788K model 3.9 ms at B=4096 (1.02 MB/s) with cpu_time/wall = 1.73, 2.95M model 6.6 ms (0.6 MB/s) with cpu_time/wall = 4.64, so BNNS did not use the 12 P-cores. A hand-parallel version is the honest multi-core baseline plan.md demands, has no device-numerics coupling (CPU results were bitwise batch-shape invariant), and needs no Core ML. AMX units are shared per core cluster, so scaling beyond ~4 threads per cluster is uncertain.
candidates.granularity: Same 2048-byte blocks; any B >= number of threads works (no batch-shape compile), so small inputs (100 KB-2 MB) are served better than by the ANE.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Back-of-envelope: 0.6 MB/s per busy thread observed -> 3-7 MB/s on 12 P-cores if AMX sharing does not bottleneck (unverified); would exceed the ANE's 1.86 MB/s.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: This is the baseline; it must be compared with the ANE's 1.45-1.86 MB/s (788K model) and 0.9 MB/s (2.95M model).
candidates.killCriterion: 12-thread run does not exceed the Core ML CPU_ONLY 1.0 MB/s by at least the noise floor (AMX contention), in which case the ANE's 1.8x stands.
candidates.firstExperiment: Swift/Accelerate step kernel for the 788K model (BNNS fp16 dense layers or vDSP/cblas_hgemm), B=4096 split across 12 threads, measure ms/step and compare with the Core ML CPU_ONLY and CPU_AND_NE numbers on the same input.

risks: Device- and OS-bound archives: the coder consumes fp16 probabilities, so an archive encoded with the ANE is decodable only by a bit-identical ANE path (ANE vs CPU logits differ by up to 3e-3; GPU conv layout is not even batch-shape invariant). An ANE compiler or macOS update that changes fp16 rounding would break decoding of older archives. A product would need a deterministic integer reference model, with the ANE used only when proven bit-identical to it; for the demo, record model hash, compute unit and B in the header and refuse to decode on a mismatch.

Modality mismatch: sub-3M models trained on enwik8 expand images/audio to 200%+ (Delétang Table 1) and generalise poorly to binaries; the demo must gate by content (byte histogram/entropy or a first-block trial) and fall back to PPMd/xz, or ship per-modality models. Ratio claims must be made on held-out data (enwik9 slices), not enwik8, and measured through the fp16 Core ML model rather than the torch model.

Speed advantage over the CPU is modest and not yet proven against a real multi-core baseline: the Core ML CPU path used only ~1.7 threads (788K) / ~4.6 threads (2.95M); a 12-thread hand-parallel BNNS/AMX implementation could reach several MB/s and beat the ANE's 1.86 MB/s. Until that is measured, the honest pitch is offload (CPU ~80% idle during ANE steps) plus 1.5-1.8x over Core ML's own CPU scheduling.

Neural decode is 100x slower than xz decode (1-2 MB/s vs 128 MB/s) and 5-6x slower than PPMd both ways; even at best the ratio gain (~25% -> ~16-18% on text) buys about 30% smaller output for a 100x decode-speed cost, which limits it to archival use cases.

Granularity: rated speed needs >= B x 2 KiB of input (8 MiB at B=4096); small files or many small entries get B in the tens and fall toward the 17 KB/s single-block speed, so the archiver must concatenate entries into a solid stream or fall back.

Encoder speed: a sequence-mode (teacher-forced) encoder would run one call per 2048 bytes instead of 2048 calls, but its fp16 accumulation order may differ from the step-mode decoder; keep the encoder step-wise (symmetric ~1-2 MB/s) or add a verification decode pass.

Measurement caveats: latencies were taken through Python predict() with fp32 one-hot inputs (input copy dominates the floor at B=16384); Swift with fp16 MLMultiArray/MLState should be faster, but the CPU-side softmax/CDF quantisation and range coding (~0.3-0.5 ms per 4096 symbols per core) are not yet measured end-to-end. The random-weight model is a latency proxy only; trained RWKV blocks (time-mix/channel-mix) have a different op mix and should be re-timed.

Training: PyTorch 2.14 MPS is present but training the 3M model (~3.6e16 FLOPs for 20 epochs of enwik8) is an estimated 2-3 hours at an assumed 3-5 TFLOPS sustained (unverified); export must go through coremltools 9 (torch 2.14 is newer than coremltools' tested 2.7.0 and emitted a warning), or through the MIL builder from numpy weights as done here.

reports.summary: The two libraries split cleanly into black boxes and modifiable Swift. Black boxes: zlib (Deflate inflate/deflate, CRC-32), libbz2 (bzip2 both directions), Apple Compression (XZ/LZMA decode, LZMA2 encode via compression_encode_buffer, LZFSE/LZVN/brotli decode), CommonCrypto/CryptoKit (AES-ECB primitive, HMAC, PBKDF2, SHA-1/256). Modifiable Swift: LZMA/LZMA2 decode, PPMd H/I, RAR3/RAR5 LZ, LHA (lh1/lh4-7/lhx/lzs/lz5), Deflate64, zstd, LZ4, StuffIt/StuffItX, Blake2sp, CRC-16, the LH5 encoder, and all chunk pipelines. Existing parallelism is coarse: GyoshukuKit's OrderedChunkPipeline runs 1 MiB deflate blocks, 4.5 MB bzip2 streams, 16 MiB LZMA2 chunks and 1 MiB LH5 chunks on up to min(cpu, 8, RAM GiB) threads; KaitoKit's only codec-level parallelism is ParallelBzip2Decompressor (byte-aligned stream starts, 8 workers), which falls back to serial on ordinary single-stream .bz2 (measured: the corpus text.tar.bz2 has 1 byte-aligned start and ~299 bit-aligned blocks, decoding at ~50 MB/s); per-entry/solid-group extraction parallelism lives in KaitoFinder's ParallelExtraction, not KaitoKit. Inherently serial stages are range decoding (LZMA, PPMd, RAR PPMd), adaptive Huffman (lh1), Huffman decode within a block, BWT inverse pointer-chasing within a bzip2 block, and the 7zAES 2^19-round SHA-256 chain; embarrassingly parallel stages are block decode when blocks are independent (xz multi-block, bzip2 blocks, LZ4 independent blocks), LZ77 match finding across positions, CRC/hash/AES-CTR/CBC-decrypt over chunks. The GPU insertion points are the closure boundaries that already exist: OrderedChunkPipeline.Encoder (DeflateBlock.encode, Bzip2StreamEncoder.encode, LZMA2Compressor.encode), LH5Encoder.write's command list before writeBlock, and Decompressor.read(into:) behind a worker like ParallelBzip2Decompressor.Workers.decode; the data crossing is 1–16 MiB blocks in, blocks or (symbol,distance) command arrays out, with a memcpy or allocator change because the current 256 KiB/1 MiB Data buffers are not page-aligned for makeBuffer(bytesNoCopy:). Recommendation: try first the CPU block-parallel XZ decoder (11 blocks × KaitoKit's own LZMA2Decoder at ~156 MB/s/core replaces Apple Compression's single-thread 140 MB/s; expected 1.9 s → ~0.3 s on text.tar.xz) because it is the largest measurable win and needs no GPU; as the GPU technical demo, do exhaustive LH5 match finding in Metal (8 KiB window fits the 32 KiB threadgroup memory, encoder is fully ours, 1 MiB chunks already exist) with a CPU reference of the same rule for byte identity; CRC-32 and AES on the GPU are predicted losers (zlib crc32 ~47 GB/s/core measured by the owner) and should be measured only to document why. ANE is limited to a batched byte-prediction demo: the owner's probe measured ≤1.49 M predictions/s, a ~1.5 MB/s ceiling, two orders of magnitude below any CPU codec.

candidates.name: Block-parallel XZ decode via the XZ index (multi-core CPU, own LZMA2Decoder)
candidates.whatItComputes: Parses the XZ stream index, splits the container into its independent blocks (each starts with an LZMA2 dictionary reset by format definition), and decodes each block's raw LZMA2 payload with KaitoKit's own LZMA2Decoder on its own core, emitting output in block order.
candidates.mapping: Not a GPU/ANE fit: LZMA range decoding is a serial adaptive-probability loop; a GPU lane would run it at a small fraction of a P-core. It is the biggest measurable win in the map because today XZDecompressor hands the whole stream to Apple Compression's compression_stream (single-threaded black box) even though xz -T0 output is multi-block. Insertion: replace/augment Sources/KaitoKit/Codecs/XZ/XZDecompressor.swift with an index parser (the TarSplice CompressedTarMapRecorder already models XZBlockMap.Block ranges) that constructs LZMA2Decoder(source:offset:compressedSize:properties:expectedSize:dictionarySizeLimit:) per block and an ordered worker pool like ParallelBzip2Decompressor.Workers; data crossing is only offsets/sizes plus per-block output buffers (~24 MiB each here), no copy of the compressed input.
candidates.granularity: One XZ block per worker; corpus text.tar.xz has 11 blocks of 24 MiB uncompressed (dict 8 MiB), so up to 11-way parallelism; single-block archives (default xz without -T) gain nothing.
candidates.expectedThroughput: ~1.0–1.4 GB/s aggregate on 11 P-cores (back-of-envelope: 156 MB/s/core measured for LZMA2 in text.7z sha × 11 blocks, less memory contention); text.tar.xz 1.915 s → ~0.25–0.35 s.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Apple Compression COMPRESSION_LZMA single stream: text.tar.xz list median 1.915 s for 268,441,600 B ≈ 140 MB/s (owner's perf/kk2/results.json).
candidates.killCriterion: xz -lvv on the archives the owner cares about shows Blocks: 1 (single-threaded xz output); then there is no parallelism to harvest and the per-block decoder only adds code.

candidates.name: Block-parallel bzip2 decode at bit-aligned block boundaries (CPU first, GPU threadgroup-per-block as the stretch)
candidates.whatItComputes: Finds the 48-bit block magic (0x314159265359) at arbitrary bit offsets, decodes each 900 kB block independently (Huffman with selectors → inverse MTF/RLE2 → inverse BWT → RLE1 → block CRC), and emits in order. GPU variant: one threadgroup per block, Huffman/iMTF decode by one or a few lanes, then iBWT pointer chase per block with many blocks in flight.
candidates.mapping: Prerequisite in either target: an own Swift bzip2 block decoder, because libbz2 cannot start mid-stream; today ParallelBzip2Decompressor only splits at byte-aligned stream starts (pbzip2-style concatenated streams) and fell back to serial libbz2 on the corpus file. Within a block the Huffman decode and the iBWT walk are serial chains (iBWT is ~900 k dependent loads through a 900 k × 4 B table; that table does not fit 32 KiB threadgroup memory so it is device-memory latency bound on the GPU); across blocks it is embarrassingly parallel (~299 blocks in the corpus). Insertion: ParallelBzip2Decompressor.Workers.decode(Data) -> Decoded is the swap point; the scanner needs a bit-level magic search instead of Bzip2StreamLayout.isStreamStart. Data crossing: compressed block (~330 kB) in, 900 kB out; block buffers must be copied into page-aligned MTLBuffers or allocated there.
candidates.granularity: One bzip2 block (100–900 kB uncompressed, level digit) per worker/threadgroup; ~299 blocks for 268 MiB at level 9.
candidates.expectedThroughput: CPU: ~500–600 MB/s on 12 P-cores (back-of-envelope: 50 MB/s/core measured serial × 12, minus the extra bit-scan). GPU: unknown; the ICPP'24 paper reports up to 2400 MB/s for iBWT+iMTF on an A100 and up to 6.1× over a multicore CPU iBWT (search snippet, unverified); scaled by memory bandwidth (~546 GB/s vs ~1.5–2 TB/s) a bandwidth-bound M4 Max ceiling would be roughly a third of that, but the per-block pointer chase is latency- not bandwidth-bound, so treat any GPU number as unmeasured.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: libbz2 serial: text.tar.bz2 list median 5.41 s for 268 MiB ≈ 50 MB/s (perf/kk2/results.json); the GPU must beat the 12-core CPU block decoder, not this serial bar.
candidates.killCriterion: If a single 900 kB block's GPU iBWT takes longer than (block count / P-core count) × the CPU per-block time — i.e. GPU aggregate < CPU-12-core aggregate on the same 299 blocks — the GPU variant is dead; the CPU variant is killed only if the bit-level magic scan plus own decoder cannot beat 50 MB/s × cores.
candidates.firstExperiment: Bit-scan text.tar.bz2 for block magics (expect ~299), decode one block with a Swift block decoder and cmp against bzip2 -dc; then a Metal kernel that performs only the iBWT pointer chase on a precomputed 900 k-entry table for 299 blocks concurrently, timed against the same loop on 12 cores.
