candidates.name: GPU exhaustive LZ77 match finding for the LH5 encoder (Metal compute, CPU Huffman emission)
candidates.whatItComputes: For every position in a 1 MiB chunk (plus 8 KiB history) finds the longest match (3…256 bytes) within the 8 KiB window with a fixed tie-break (nearest distance), producing a (length, distance) pair per position; the CPU then does greedy or lazy parsing and the existing LH5Encoder.writeBlock Huffman emission.
candidates.mapping: Best GPU demo in the map: the encoder is our Swift (LH5Encoder.swift), window is 8 KiB so the whole window plus lookahead fits the 32 KiB threadgroup memory, and GyoshukuKit already cuts LHA input into 1 MiB chunks with 8 KiB history for OrderedChunkPipeline (LHAWriter.compressionChunkSize). Match finding is embarrassingly parallel across positions (one lane per position, SIMD-32 lanes compare against the same window). Byte identity: the current CPU path uses a 256-probe hash chain, so a GPU exhaustive search produces different (equal-or-better) bytes; define identity against a CPU reference implementing the same exhaustive rule. Insertion: inside LH5Encoder.write(_:startingAt:to:) between the match loop and writeBlock — the GPU returns the Command list (symbol, position) for the chunk. Data crossing: 1 MiB + 8 KiB in; up to 1 M commands out (4 bytes each packed → 4 MiB worst case); the Data chunk must be copied into a page-aligned MTLBuffer unless the pipeline allocates chunks with posix_memalign.
candidates.granularity: 1 MiB chunk with 8 KiB history per dispatch; ≥ 8 chunks in flight to hide command-buffer latency.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Back-of-envelope: 1 Mi positions × up to 8192 candidates ≈ 8.6 G candidate checks per MiB; 40 cores × 128 lanes × 1.68 GHz ≈ 8.6 T lane-ops/s → a few ms per MiB with early exits, i.e. ~0.3–1 GB/s of match finding; CPU emission afterwards is the likely limiter (unmeasured, estimate 200–400 MB/s/core).
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: LH5Encoder on CPU: text256 1 thread 4.656 s (57.6 MB/s), 8 threads 1.005 s (267 MB/s) with byte-identical output (GyoshukuKit verification 2026-09-26-p4ga-parallel-lh5.tsv); Benchmarks run: lha text 4 threads 1.31 s wall / 5.0 s user.
candidates.killCriterion: GPU match finding plus CPU emission for 256 MiB text is slower than the 8-thread CPU LH5 (1.0 s), or the GPU kernel alone exceeds ~4 ms per MiB (it would then be no better than 8 CPU cores of the existing hash chain).
candidates.firstExperiment: Metal kernel over one 1 MiB chunk of text256.txt returning (length, distance) per position; validate against a brute-force Swift reference; time 256 dispatches; feed the commands into LH5Encoder.writeBlock and verify KaitoKit's LHAStaticHuffmanDecoder round-trips the bytes.

candidates.name: GPU AES-CTR keystream / AES-CBC decrypt (WinZip AES, 7zAES, RAR5)
candidates.whatItComputes: AES-256 block encryption of counter blocks (WinZip CTR keystream) or CBC decryption (each block = AES-decrypt(C_i) XOR C_{i-1}), both embarrassingly parallel across 16-byte blocks.
candidates.mapping: Maps trivially (independent blocks), but the CPU has ARMv8 AES instructions behind CommonCrypto; KaitoKit already structures both modes as parallel ECB calls (WinZipAES makeKeyStream builds counter blocks and calls CommonCryptoPrimitives.aesECBEncrypt; AESCBCRandomAccess decrypts ranges via aesECBDecrypt + XOR in Swift), so the insertion point exists: CommonCryptoPrimitives.aesECB(_:blocks:key:). A GPU T-table AES without hardware AES is expected to lose to per-core AES instructions once dispatch and buffer copies are counted; the decrypted bytes still feed a serial decoder. The 7zAES key derivation (2^19 chained SHA-256) is inherently serial and not a target.
candidates.granularity: 256 KiB reads (AESCBCRandomAccess.maximumReadSize) and 4096-block CTR batches today; GPU would need ≥ several MiB per dispatch.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Unverified; GPU AES on discrete GPUs is reported in the tens of GB/s (literature, unverified), while CommonCrypto AES-256 with hardware instructions is expected in the several-GB/s-per-core range (unverified; accel-lab baseline aes-ctr-commoncrypto / aes-cbc-decrypt-commoncrypto will give the bar). text-enc.7z vs text.7z sha differ by only 0.14 s for 80 MB of ciphertext plus KDF, so AES is already a minor share.

candidates.name: GPU Huffman/LZ decode of existing Deflate, Deflate64, LHA and RAR streams (self-synchronising or gap-array decode)
candidates.whatItComputes: Decodes a canonical-Huffman bitstream in parallel by starting lanes at arbitrary bit offsets and exploiting self-synchronisation (or a gap array written by the encoder), then resolves LZ77 back-references in a second pass.
candidates.mapping: Poor fit for reading archives we did not write: Deflate/LHA/RAR block boundaries and code tables are only known after serially parsing the stream; self-synchronisation works per Huffman table but the LZ77 back-reference pass has prefix dependencies (Gompresso removed them only by changing the format, +15–30% size per the ACEAPEX summary). Gap arrays require encoder cooperation, so they apply only to GyoshukuKit-written Deflate/LH5 read back by KaitoKit — a closed loop with little user value. CPU bars are already high: zlib inflate ~733 MB/s single core on text.tar.gz, and multi-entry archives are extracted per-entry in parallel by KaitoFinder. Insertion would be a new Decompressor behind Decompressor.read(into:) with a block-table pre-pass; data crossing is the whole compressed entry plus its output.
candidates.granularity: Whole compressed stream per dispatch (tables must be resolved first); 128 KiB–1 MiB Huffman blocks internally.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Unmeasured. Weißenberger & Schmidt report >10× over zstd's CPU Huffman decoder on TITAN-class GPUs and later work >100 GB/s for Huffman-only decode (search snippets, unverified); those are Huffman-only figures on far higher-bandwidth GPUs and exclude LZ77 resolution.

candidates.name: LZMA/LZMA2, PPMd (7z, ZIP method 98, RAR3), RAR3/RAR5 LZ, lh1 adaptive Huffman on GPU
candidates.whatItComputes: Range decoding with adaptive binary probabilities (LZMA), PPM context-model updates (PPMd H/I), and RAR's block-adaptive LZ; all are single sequential state machines.
candidates.mapping: Inherently serial: every decoded bit updates probabilities that the next bit depends on, and PPMd mutates a suballocator arena per symbol. Chunk-level parallelism exists only at LZMA2 dictionary resets, and the corpus text.7z (7zz -mx6) has 1618 LZMA2 chunks but exactly one dictionary reset — so nothing to parallelise for a typical solid 7z. LZMA2Decoder already tracks reset points (LZMA2ResetPoint / LZMA2ResetTracker) but uses them only for backward seeks in SevenZipFolderCoordinator. GPU lanes execute such loops at a small fraction of a P-core (divergent, latency-bound; unverified generic claim). Multi-folder 7z and per-entry RAR already parallelise at the entry/solid-group level in KaitoFinder.
candidates.granularity: Per dictionary reset (7z: rarely more than one per folder); per 7z folder / RAR solid group otherwise.
candidates.expectedThroughput: No gain expected. CPU today: LZMA2 ~156 MB/s (text.7z), PPMd var.I ~14 MB/s and var.H ~9 MB/s (KaitoKit verification records), RAR5 34–71 MB/s on the 50k-file corpus.

candidates.name: ANE byte-prediction model + CPU arithmetic coder (neural lossless compression demo)
candidates.whatItComputes: A small fp16 network (MLP/LSTM/Transformer) predicts a probability distribution over the next byte for thousands of independent blocks per Core ML prediction; a Swift arithmetic/range coder encodes each block's bytes with those probabilities, and decoding reruns the identical model.
candidates.mapping: The only way to involve the ANE, since Core ML exposes no integer or bitwise ops on it and everything runs in fp16. It fits only as a batch: input [blocks × context] per prediction, recurrent state in MLState; per-byte calls are dominated by the ~0.1 ms Core ML dispatch floor (owner's batch=1 probe: 0.109 ms). The owner's probes already measured the ceiling: 1.49 M predictions/s at batch 4096 (h1024, 4 layers) and 0.84 M/s for the trained MLP at batch 1024, i.e. ~1.5 MB/s if one prediction codes one byte. Placement must be proven per op with MLComputePlan; the GPU fallback (also fp16) is not an ANE result. Insertion: a new codec, not a stage of any existing one; data crossing is context windows of all blocks per call (e.g. 4096 × 64 bytes).
candidates.granularity: Batch of 1024–4096 independent blocks (e.g. 64 KiB each) per Core ML call; contexts of 64 bytes.
candidates.expectedThroughput: ≤ ~1.5 MB/s encode and decode (owner measured 1,487,404 predictions/s best case), two orders of magnitude below xz decode (140 MB/s) and slower than PPMd; compression ratio unknown until measured — must clearly beat xz -6's 0.309 on text256 to have any story.

candidates.name: GPU forward BWT (suffix sorting) for bzip2 compression, CPU MTF/RLE/Huffman
candidates.whatItComputes: Sorts the rotations of each 900 kB block on the GPU (radix/merge-based suffix sort per block, many blocks concurrently) and returns the BWT string plus origin pointer; libbz2-equivalent MTF, RLE2, Huffman table selection and bit emission run on the CPU.
candidates.mapping: The block sort is the dominant cost of bzip2 compression and is a well-studied GPU workload (block-independent, sort-based), while the remaining stages are serial per block but cheap. Fits GyoshukuKit's ParallelBzip2Compressor, which already produces one complete bzip2 stream per 4.5 MB chunk through Bzip2StreamEncoder.encode(_:level:) — the OrderedChunkPipeline.Encoder closure is the insertion point; a GPU path replaces libbz2 with own Swift stages after the BWT. Output bytes differ from libbz2 (Huffman table selection heuristics), so identity means "decodes to the same bytes" plus a CPU reference of the same encoder. Data crossing: 900 kB block in, 900 kB BWT + index out; sort scratch of several × 4 B per byte in device memory.
candidates.granularity: 900 kB block per sort; ≥ 12 blocks in flight (a 4.5 MB chunk holds 5).
candidates.expectedThroughput: Unmeasured on Apple GPUs. Literature: 60–150 MB/s suffix sorting on enwik8 (older GPUs) and up to 460 MB/s BWT on a GTX 1080 Ti (search snippets, unverified); expect a few hundred MB/s of BWT on the M4 Max at best, then CPU stages at an estimated 100+ MB/s per core.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: libbz2 compress level 9: small tbz 8 threads 1.98 s wall / 7.29 s user for 127,987,190 B ≈ 65 MB/s wall, ~17.6 MB/s per core; headers tbz 0.32 s wall / 1.63 s user (Benchmarks results.tsv run.UZMslT).
candidates.killCriterion: GPU BWT of 900 kB blocks below ~200 MB/s aggregate (then 12 CPU cores of libbz2 at ~17.6 MB/s each ≈ 210 MB/s already match it), or the own Swift MTF/Huffman stages costing more than the sort.

facts.fact: GyoshukuKit encoders: ZIP/tar.gz Deflate via zlib in 1 MiB DeflateBlock units with a 32 KiB previous-block dictionary and SYNC_FLUSH; tar.bz2 via libbz2 one complete stream per 5×level×100,000-byte chunk; 7z and tar.xz LZMA2 via Apple compression_encode_buffer(COMPRESSION_LZMA) per 16 MiB chunk (4 MiB packing for tar.xz members) re-framed by XZLZMA2.extract into raw LZMA2; LHA LH5 via an own Swift hash-chain encoder (8 KiB window, 256 probes, 32,768 commands per Huffman block) in 1 MiB chunks with 8 KiB history; AES via CommonCrypto (CTR through ECB, HMAC-SHA1, PBKDF2 1000 iterations); 7z key = 2^19 chained SHA-256 (CryptoKit).

OrderedChunkPipeline (GyoshukuKit) runs Encoder closures on a concurrent DispatchQueue with threads = compressionThreads ?? max(1, min(activeProcessorCount, 8, physicalMemory GiB)); it holds at most 2×threads+1 items and blocks the caller before allocating the next input. LZMA2ChunkPipeline, ParallelBzip2Compressor, ParallelXZCompressor, GzipCompressor/DeflateBlock, LHAWriter and ZipReencryption key derivation all use it.

KaitoKit's only codec-level parallelism is ParallelBzip2Decompressor: it scans for byte-aligned stream starts (BZh[1-9] + block/EOS magic), decodes up to 8 intervals of ≤8 MiB compressed / ≤16 MiB output with libbz2 workers, and falls back to the serial Bzip2Decompressor when no candidate appears within the limit. KaitoKit itself has no parallel extraction; it exposes ArchiveReader.reopen() and ArchiveEntry.solidGroup, and KaitoFinder's ParallelExtraction uses ≤ min(activeProcessorCount, 8) workers over per-entry / per-solid-group buckets.

The perf corpus text.tar.bz2 (bsdtar -cjf, 100,330,406 B) contains exactly 1 byte-aligned bzip2 stream start and ~299 bit-aligned block magics, so ParallelBzip2Decompressor decodes it serially; its list median is 5.41 s for 268 MiB ≈ 50 MB/s.

text.tar.xz (xz -6 -T0) has 1 stream and 11 independent blocks of 25,165,824 B (last 16,783,360 B), lzma2 dict=8MiB, CRC64; KaitoKit decodes it with Apple Compression in a single thread: list median 1.915 s ≈ 140 MB/s.

text.7z (7zz a -mx6) contains 1618 LZMA2 chunks and exactly 1 dictionary reset over 268,435,456 unpacked bytes, so LZMA2 reset points offer no parallelism for this archive; KaitoKit's LZMA2Decoder tracks reset points only for backward seeks. kaito sha median 1.719 s ≈ 156 MB/s including SHA-256 of the output.

risks: Byte-identity rule: any GPU match finder (LH5, Deflate) or own bzip2 encoder produces bytes different from the current zlib/libbz2/hash-chain output; the plan's 'byte identical to CPU path' must be defined against a CPU reference of the same algorithm (and 'decodes to identical bytes'), or every compression candidate is dead on arrival.

Zero-copy Metal needs page-aligned, page-multiple allocations for makeBuffer(bytesNoCopy:); KaitoKit's 256 KiB Data/[UInt8] staging buffers and GyoshukuKit's 1 MiB Data blocks are not, so each candidate pays a memcpy per block or changes the allocator at the pipeline boundary — measure this before quoting any GPU speedup.

Command-buffer round-trip latency (order 0.1 ms, unverified) versus the 256 KiB pull granularity of Decompressor.read(into:) means GPU stages must be batched (≥ several MiB, many blocks in flight) behind a worker pool like ParallelBzip2Decompressor.Workers, adding memory (already capped at (W+2)×24 MiB there).
Threadgroup memory is 32 KiB: exactly the Deflate window with no room for hash tables; only LH5's 8 KiB window fits on-chip, which is why it is the recommended GPU demo and Deflate is riskier.

Range coders and PPMd cannot be parallelised; solid 7z from 7zz -mx6 has a single dictionary reset (measured), so no GPU or multi-core gain exists for the slowest read paths (7z LZMA2 156 MB/s, PPMd 9–14 MB/s) except across folders/entries, which KaitoFinder already does.

Most real .bz2 files are single-stream (bsdtar, bzip2 CLI), so the existing byte-aligned ParallelBzip2Decompressor gives no speedup on them; block parallelism requires an own Swift bzip2 block decoder with a bit-level magic scan (libbz2 cannot start mid-stream), a non-trivial correctness surface (selectors, MTF, RLE2, iBWT, block CRC).

ANE: fp16-only execution and Core ML dispatch overhead (~0.1 ms per call measured at batch 1) cap a neural codec at ~1.5 MB/s; encoder and decoder must reproduce identical probabilities, which is only safe on the same device and OS build, and MLComputePlan may silently place ops on GPU/CPU — a GPU-run LSTM is not an ANE result.

Discrete-GPU literature numbers (A100/H100, 1.5–3 TB/s HBM) do not transfer; scale by ~546 GB/s and by the latency-bound nature of per-block pointer chasing before citing any expectation, and label them back-of-envelope.
The AES/SHA/LZFSE/LZ4/memcpy CPU bars from accel-lab baseline have not been produced yet (Baseline.swift exists, no TSV in Results/); the AES and LZ4 kill criteria depend on them.

The largest measurable win (block-parallel XZ decode) is CPU-only and does not support the GPU/NPU narrative; it should still be reported first because it is what users would notice, and it changes the multi-core baseline the GPU must beat for XZ.

GyoshukuKit's slowest stage is Apple's LZMA2 encoder (~2 MB/s per core, 33.9 s for 256 MiB 7z at 4 threads); a GPU match finder cannot help unless an own Swift LZMA range encoder is written, which is a product-scale effort outside the demo.

Perf-run hygiene: kk2 results used 2 rounds; noise floors must be re-established base-vs-base on an idle machine before any GPU-vs-CPU claim, per the owner's plan (release, same input, alternating, medians).

reports.summary: Nothing in Apple's compression stack leaves the CPU: on this macOS 27.2 machine libcompression.dylib links only liblzma and libSystem, libAppleArchive.dylib links libbz2/liblzma/libcompression/CoreFoundation/Security/libSystem, an LZFSE encode loads no IOKit/Metal/ANE images, ioreg shows no compression IOService, and no Apple document or WWDC session claims a compression engine, so the "hardware-assisted LZFSE on M1" folklore is unsupported and there is no third-party-visible compression engine on M4 Max. The CPU bars measured here (M4 Max, 12P+4E, 256 MiB, medians) are high: CRC-32 via system zlib (KaitoKit's actual path) 40.8 GB/s on one core and 238 GB/s on 16 threads; AES-256 keystream by ECB on prebuilt counters (the WinZip path) 14.7 GB/s/core and 114 GB/s on 16 threads; but the serial HMAC-SHA1 that ZIP AE-2 requires runs at 3.1 GB/s and AES-CBC encrypt (7z/RAR) at 1.8 GB/s, and those serial stages, not AES itself, bound encrypted archives. The GPU reads 256 MiB at 311 GB/s device-side but a dispatch round trip costs 127-165 us, so CRC-32 and AES on the GPU are predicted losses and should be measured only to document why. SME is real and reachable from C today (SVL 512 bit, 4.0 int8 TOPS or 2.0 fp32 TFLOP/s per thread, shared per cluster, and armv9 -march flags SIGILL because M4 has SME without SVE); Accelerate exposes nothing byte-level beyond vImage histograms. Metal 4 on M4 Max gives MTLTensor with UInt8/Int8/Int32 types, MPP matmul2d compiles for int8->int32 and bf16/half, 32-bit atomics only, 32 KiB threadgroup memory, and tensor ops run on ordinary shader ALUs (14.8 fp16 TFLOP/s; no neural accelerators before M5); MPSGraph has bitwise AND/OR/XOR/NOT/shift/popcount and gather on UInt8/Int32 but only as whole-graph dispatches. The ANE is fp16, static-graph, Core ML-only, with ~190 us per dispatch (measured on M1 in the cited guide), so a byte predictor is viable only when thousands of independent blocks are batched per inference and placement is proven with MLComputePlan. Recommended first experiments, in order: (1) a GPU byte histogram already measured at 82 GB/s versus 38 GB/s on 16 CPU threads, the one byte-level kernel with a demonstrated win, to be checked against its share of encode time; (2) one GPU thread decoding one LZ4 block serially versus one CPU core, the discriminating number for any block-parallel decode; (3) the ANE/GPU batched byte-predictor versus a one-thread SME predictor, the CPU alternative that has no dispatch cost.

candidates.name: GPU CRC-32 (chunked CRC with GF(2) combine)
candidates.whatItComputes: CRC-32 (ISO-HDLC, used by ZIP/gzip/LHA/7z) of an entire buffer: each thread/threadgroup CRCs its own slice, then slices are merged with crc32_combine-style polynomial shifts (as zlib does) either on the GPU in a second pass or on the CPU.
candidates.mapping: Maps trivially in shape (embarrassingly parallel over slices, 32-bit integer math, 32-bit atomics available) and the GPU can stream the input at 311 GB/s device-side, but the work per byte is tiny, the CPU already has a PMULL/CRC-instruction path at 40.8 GB/s per core, a Metal dispatch costs 127-165 us round trip, and in the real pipelines CRC is computed on bytes the CPU is already touching (decoder output), so it is hidden under decompression. Predicted loss; measure only to document.
candidates.granularity: Whole buffers of at least ~64 MiB to amortise the 165 us dispatch (at 238 GB/s CPU that is already ~40 MB of work); slices of 4-64 KiB per threadgroup; the 32-bit-atomics-only limit means the combine step is a tree, not an atomic.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Upper bound 311 GB/s (measured GPU read rate of 256 MiB, gpuStartTime/gpuEndTime); realistic 150-250 GB/s after the combine pass and dispatch (back-of-envelope: 256 MiB / 0.86 ms read + 0.165 ms dispatch = 250 GB/s wall). CPU 16-thread bar is 238 GB/s, so at best parity on 256 MiB buffers and a loss below ~32 MiB.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: KaitoKit CRC32.swift wraps system zlib crc32: measured 40.8 GB/s single thread, 238 GB/s on 16 threads with crc32_combine (256 MiB, medians). Raw __crc32d one chain 10.5 GB/s, three chains 31.5 GB/s. GyoshukuKit uses the same updateCRC path.
candidates.killCriterion: If the CRC stage is less than ~5% of decode/encode wall in a profile of the perf corpus (it runs at 40.8 GB/s per core against decoders at 0.4-5 GB/s per core), no GPU CRC can move the total; also killed outright if the GPU wall including dispatch on 256 MiB is not below the 16-thread CPU median (238 GB/s = 1.13 ms).
candidates.firstExperiment: Reuse the xor_reduce Metal harness in the scratchpad: replace XOR with a per-thread table-less CRC (bitwise or 4-bit table in threadgroup memory) over 256-byte slices, write per-threadgroup CRCs, combine on CPU with zlib crc32_combine; compare wall (commit to completed) with the 16-thread zlib number and check byte equality of the result.

candidates.name: GPU AES keystream / AES-CTR for WinZip AE-2 and AES-CBC decrypt for 7z/RAR
candidates.whatItComputes: AES-256 block encryption of counter blocks (little-endian 128-bit counter starting at 1 for WinZip AE-2) XORed into data; or AES-CBC decryption of 7z/RAR5 streams (each block depends only on its own ciphertext and the previous ciphertext block, so decrypt is parallel; encrypt is a serial chain).
candidates.mapping: AES rounds are 32-bit integer/table work that maps to SIMD lanes (T-table in 32 KiB threadgroup memory fits: 4 KiB per table), fully parallel across blocks, memory streaming at up to 311 GB/s. But the CPU has AES instructions (FEAT_AES) reaching 14.7 GB/s per core on the exact ECB-on-counters path the repos use and 114 GB/s on 16 threads, and the formats add a serial authenticator: ZIP AE-2 HMAC-SHA1 over every ciphertext byte at 3.1 GB/s single thread cannot be split, and 7z/RAR AES-CBC encryption is a serial chain at 1.8 GB/s. The GPU could at best remove a stage that is already 5x faster than the stage that bounds the pipeline.
candidates.granularity: Whole encrypted members or multi-MiB spans; per-thread 16-byte blocks; the keystream must be aligned to the format's counter (WinZip: LE counter, first value 1; GyoshukuKit IOChunk-sized pieces).
candidates.expectedThroughput: Back-of-envelope: 256 MiB at 311 GB/s read+write bound is ~1.7 ms plus 0.165 ms dispatch, i.e. up to ~140 GB/s, roughly parity with 16 CPU threads (114 GB/s ECB keystream); against a single CPU thread (14.7 GB/s) it would be ~8x, but the HMAC-SHA1 stage (3.1 GB/s) makes the ZIP pipeline finish no faster.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Measured: AES-256 ECB keystream on prebuilt LE counters (CCCrypt, the ZipAESEncryptor/WinZipAES path) 14.7 GB/s 1T, 114 GB/s 16T; CommonCrypto AES-256-CTR (BE counter only, so an upper bound for WinZip) 13.7 GB/s 1T, 98 GB/s 16T; AES-128-CTR 18.0 GB/s 1T; AES-256-CBC encrypt 1.82 GB/s 1T, CBC decrypt 16.8 GB/s 1T; HMAC-SHA1 3.12 GB/s, HMAC-SHA256 3.10 GB/s, SHA-256 3.02 GB/s 1T; 64-bit XOR loop 47.8 GB/s 1T (GyoshukuKit XORs per byte in Swift; that loop is a CPU-side fix, not a GPU problem).
candidates.killCriterion: HMAC-SHA1 at 3.1 GB/s single thread is a serial dependency over the whole ciphertext of a ZIP entry and 7z/RAR encrypt is a 1.8 GB/s serial CBC chain: unless the demo targets only decrypt of unauthenticated 7z/RAR CBC data, no GPU AES speedup changes end-to-end wall. Also killed if the GPU keystream on 256 MiB is not below the 114 GB/s 16-thread CPU median.
candidates.firstExperiment: Metal kernel: 32-bit T-table AES-256 in threadgroup memory, each thread encrypts 4 counter blocks and XORs into a device buffer; verify against CCCrypt ECB output on the same counters; time 256 MiB wall vs 14.7 GB/s (1T) and 114 GB/s (16T). Then profile a real AE-2 ZIP write to show the HMAC-SHA1 stage dominating.

candidates.name: Block-parallel decode of already-independent units (LZ4 independent blocks, bzip2 blocks, XZ blocks, zstd frames, GyoshukuKit tar chunks) on the GPU
candidates.whatItComputes: Runs one serial decoder instance per independent compressed unit, thousands at once, each thread (or small group) decoding its own block: LZ4 sequences (token, literals, 16-bit offset copies), bzip2 blocks (BWT inverse + MTF + Huffman), XZ blocks (LZMA2 range decoding), zstd frames (FSE/Huffman + sequences).
candidates.mapping: This is the only decode shape that fits a GPU: no cross-thread dependency inside a unit, parallelism from the count of units. It fits badly in every other way: byte-granular, branchy, table-lookup-heavy code with serial dependency per byte; a GPU scalar thread is many times slower than a P-core; 32 KiB threadgroup memory cannot hold a 64 KiB LZ4 window, a 900 KiB bzip2 block or a multi-MiB LZMA dictionary, so state lives in device memory; SIMD width 32 means divergence within a simdgroup wastes lanes; output size per unit is unknown until decoded (needs prefix-sum of sizes or a bounded scratch). nvCOMP-style GPU LZ4 exists on CUDA with 64 KiB chunks; the equivalent on Metal is unbuilt. XZ blocks from ParallelXZCompressor are 16 MiB each (chunks inside a block share the dictionary and are not independent); bzip2 blocks inside a stream are not byte aligned, so block starts must be found by bit-offset magic search; KaitoKit today decodes XZ through one compression_stream and zstd serially, and parallelises bzip2 only at byte-aligned stream starts.
candidates.granularity: At least ~1,000-10,000 independent units of 16-256 KiB (nvCOMP uses 64 KiB chunks) to fill 40 cores x 32 lanes with slack for divergence; the repos' natural units are far coarser: XZ blocks 16 MiB (ParallelXZCompressor.defaultBlockSize), bzip2 chunks 500 KB x level (ParallelBzip2Compressor), LZ4 frame blocks 64 KiB-4 MiB with the independence flag (flags & 32) required, zstd frames as written by pzstd (not by GyoshukuKit).
candidates.expectedThroughput: Unmeasured on Metal; the discriminating number is the single-GPU-thread serial LZ4 decode rate, expected in the 10-100 MB/s range per thread (back-of-envelope: a few instructions per byte at ~1.5 GHz with device-memory latency per access), i.e. aggregate 5-30 GB/s only with >1,000 live threads and 64 KiB units. CUDA reference points: GPULZ reports 16.4 GB/s (A4000) and 29.1 GB/s (A100) decode and cites nvCOMP LZ4 at 21.1 GB/s on A4000 (unverified: taken from a search snippet of arXiv 2304.07342); the 173 GB/s B200 LZ4 figure is a fixed-function decompression engine, not a shader result, and must not be used as a GPU expectation.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Apple Compression LZ4 decode 5.33 GB/s single thread on a 34 MiB SDK-headers tar (4.1x ratio), LZFSE 3.37 GB/s, zlib 1.36 GB/s, LZMA(xz) 0.41 GB/s; multiplied by 16 threads when units are independent (xz: ~6.5 GB/s; LZ4: ~80 GB/s back-of-envelope). KaitoKit's own Swift LZ4/zstd/LZMA decoders were not measured here and are the true baseline; a CPU multi-block XZ reader (16 x 0.41 GB/s) does not exist in KaitoKit yet and is the cheaper competitor to any GPU XZ attempt.
candidates.killCriterion: If one GPU thread decodes one 64 KiB LZ4 block slower than 1/40 of one CPU core (i.e. below ~130 MB/s when the CPU does 5.3 GB/s), the GPU cannot beat 16 CPU threads even with perfect occupancy (40 cores x 32 lanes x 130 MB/s = 166 GB/s peak only under zero divergence and no memory stalls, and real lane efficiency for LZ decode is typically 10-30%). For XZ/bzip2 the kill is simpler: a CPU multi-block decoder at 16 x single-thread rate is faster to build; if it exists, the GPU must beat it.
candidates.firstExperiment: Write a serial LZ4 block decoder in MSL (token/literal/match loop, device-memory in/out), dispatch exactly 1 thread on one independent 64 KiB block from an LZ4 frame produced with block independence, verify bytes against KaitoKit's LZ4BlockDecoder, and record bytes/second for 1 thread, then 32, 1024 and 8192 blocks; compare with Apple Compression LZ4 (5.33 GB/s 1T) and with 16 CPU threads on the same blocks.

candidates.name: GPU byte histogram / symbol frequency counting for Huffman table construction
candidates.whatItComputes: 256-bin (or larger for LZ77 literal/length alphabets) frequency counts over a block, the first step of building Deflate, LH5 and zstd Huffman tables; also usable for bzip2 MTF symbol frequencies.
candidates.mapping: Fits well: pure streaming reads, per-threadgroup 256-bin counters in threadgroup memory with 32-bit atomics, one device-atomic merge per threadgroup; measured at 82 GB/s on 256 MiB of skewed text-like bytes, a 2.2x win over 16 CPU threads. The catch is placement: Deflate/LH5 count symbols after LZ77 parsing (literals plus length/distance codes), not raw bytes, so the GPU can only count if the parse already lives in GPU memory; counting raw bytes only helps order-0 coders.
candidates.granularity: Blocks of at least ~16 MiB per dispatch to amortise 165 us (at 82 GB/s a 1 MiB block takes 13 us of GPU time versus 165 us round trip); Deflate blocks are 16-64 KiB and LH5 blocks 8 KiB, so per-block counting must be batched over thousands of blocks in one dispatch.
candidates.expectedThroughput: 82 GB/s measured (256 MiB, threadgroup atomics, 256 B per thread) versus CPU 4.78 GB/s 1T and 38.0 GB/s 16T (C, 8 sub-tables). Realistic in-pipeline gain: zero unless the LZ77 parse is also on the GPU, because frequency counting is a few percent of encode time (zlib level 6 encodes at 0.137 GB/s per core; counting at 4.8 GB/s per core is <3% of that).
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Measured C 8-sub-table histogram 4.78 GB/s single thread, 32.8 GB/s 12T, 38.0 GB/s 16T; naive Swift 4.6 GB/s 1T. vImageHistogramCalculation_Planar8 (Accelerate) is the packaged CPU alternative and was not measured.
candidates.killCriterion: Profile GyoshukuKit DeflateCompressor/LH5Encoder: if frequency counting is under ~5% of encode wall (expected, since zlib level 6 runs at 0.137 GB/s per core against 4.8 GB/s counting), or if per-block counts must be returned to the CPU per block (165 us each), the kernel cannot improve archive encode time and stays a demo of a byte-level GPU primitive.
candidates.firstExperiment: Already run: hist.swift in the scratchpad (82 GB/s, results match CPU). Next: instrument GyoshukuKit's Deflate/LH5 encoders to measure the share of time spent counting, and try one dispatch that histograms 4,096 separate 64 KiB blocks into 4,096 tables (output 4 MiB) to see whether per-block tables keep the rate.

candidates.name: GPU LZ77 match finding (hash-chain / hash-table candidate search) feeding a CPU entropy coder
candidates.whatItComputes: For every position in a block, the best (or a good) match offset/length within the window, produced as a parallel candidate list; the CPU then does the greedy/lazy parse and Huffman/range coding, or the GPU does a block-local parse.
candidates.mapping: Hashing and candidate verification are parallel across positions and 32-bit integer work, and unified memory means the CPU coder can read the candidate array without copies. It does not map to the serial greedy parse (each match consumes positions), to windows larger than 32 KiB threadgroup memory (LZ4 64 KiB, Deflate 32 KiB just fits, LZMA2 MiBs do not), or to zlib-compatible output determinism (output need only be valid, not identical, which is allowed for an encoder). Prior GPU work (GPULZ, nvCOMP) does block-local LZSS/LZ4 compression with tens of GB/s on NVIDIA; nothing equivalent exists on Metal.
candidates.granularity: Independent blocks of 32-256 KiB (window-bounded), thousands per dispatch; the GyoshukuKit pipelines already cut tar input into 16 MiB (xz) and ~2.5 MB (bzip2 level 5) chunks that could be sub-blocked.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Unmeasured. Back-of-envelope: hashing 256 MiB of 4-byte windows at 311 GB/s read is ~1 ms, but candidate verification and match-length extension are latency-bound random reads; expect 5-30 GB/s of input for an LZ4-quality match finder (GPULZ reports 16-29 GB/s decode and 'up to 272x' encode speedups vs prior GPU work on A4000, no absolute GB/s verified here). The real question is whether the CPU-side coder then becomes the bottleneck: zlib level 6 at 0.137 GB/s per core is dominated by matching, so a GPU match list could raise Deflate encode by several times per core, but 16 cores of zlib already give ~2.2 GB/s.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Apple Compression zlib encode 0.137 GB/s 1T (6.8x ratio) and LZ4 encode 1.25 GB/s 1T (4.1x) on the SDK-headers tar; LZFSE 0.195 GB/s; LZMA 0.006 GB/s (11x). GyoshukuKit uses system zlib for ZIP Deflate and its own Swift LZMA2/LH5 encoders (not measured here); multiply single-thread rates by 12-16 for the chunked parallel pipelines.
candidates.killCriterion: If a GPU match finder plus CPU coding on 16 MiB chunks does not beat 16 CPU threads of zlib level 6 (~2.2 GB/s wall, back-of-envelope from 0.137 GB/s x 16) at equal or better ratio on the perf corpus, or if the candidate-array traffic (8-16 bytes per input byte) exceeds the compressed output's savings, stop. Also stop if the per-core Deflate encoder is not actually match-bound in a profile.
candidates.firstExperiment: MSL kernel: per position hash of 4 bytes into a per-block 32 KiB threadgroup hash table (Deflate window), emit best match (offset,length) per position for 4,096 blocks of 32 KiB in one dispatch; measure GB/s of input processed and compare candidate quality (sum of match lengths) against zlib's longest_match on the same blocks; then feed the candidates to a simple greedy parse plus zlib's fixed Huffman coding and compare output size and wall against zlib level 1 and 6.

candidates.name: GPU parallel Huffman / entropy decoding via self-synchronisation or gap arrays
candidates.whatItComputes: Decodes a Huffman-coded bitstream with many threads by starting each thread at an arbitrary bit offset and relying on prefix-code self-synchronisation (or on a stored 'gap array' of per-subsequence skip counts) to recover the codeword boundary, then stitching.
candidates.mapping: Fits when the container stores the side information (gap arrays add one byte per subsequence) or when self-synchronisation can be verified; Deflate, LH5, bzip2 and zstd Huffman streams store no such index, Deflate blocks are only found by decoding, and the LZ77 stage after Huffman is still serial per block, so this only pays inside a format the owner controls (e.g. a demo container or a GyoshukuKit-written chunk with an index). On NVIDIA these decoders reach a few GB/s per GPU and are used for cuSZ, not general archives.
candidates.granularity: Subsequences of 32-4,096 codewords with a stored gap array (1 byte each), thousands per dispatch; the compressed side needs an index the existing archive formats lack.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Unmeasured on Metal; cited CUDA work reports 3.64x over cuSZ's decoder on a V100 and 1.5-1.65x between the two approaches without absolute GB/s in the fetched abstracts; expect single-digit GB/s of decoded output on M4 Max, comparable to one to two CPU cores of zstd/Deflate decode.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Apple Compression zlib (Deflate) decode 1.36 GB/s 1T, LZFSE 3.37 GB/s 1T on the SDK tar; KaitoKit's Swift Deflate64/zstd/LH5 decoders not measured here.
candidates.killCriterion: No existing archive format the repos read carries codeword-boundary side information, so the candidate is dead for decompression of foreign archives; for owner-controlled containers it is dead if the stitched GPU decode of 256 MiB does not beat 16 CPU threads of Apple Compression zlib decode (~22 GB/s back-of-envelope from 1.36 GB/s x 16) or if the gap array costs more than 1% of compressed size.

candidates.name: ANE byte-predictor (small LSTM/Transformer) driving a CPU arithmetic coder (neural lossless compression)
candidates.whatItComputes: For each byte position, a probability distribution over the next byte given a context window, computed on the Neural Engine through a Core ML model; the CPU turns the probabilities into an arithmetic/range code (encode) or decodes with the same predictions (decode).
candidates.mapping: The ANE is fp16-only, executes a static graph with no data-dependent control flow, no integer bitwise ops, no gather, and is reachable only through Core ML; a byte predictor as batched matmuls does fit that shape, and int8-int8 activation paths exist on M4 per coremltools docs (the ANE guide, measured on M1/M5, says int8 weights are reconstructed to fp16, so the two sources conflict and MLComputePlan plus timing must settle it). The per-dispatch cost (~190 us on M1, 98% software/firmware overhead) kills per-byte inference (~5 KB/s); the design must batch thousands of independent blocks as one input [blocks x context] and hold recurrence in MLState. Decoding is inherently serial per block (each byte needs the previous prediction), so the batch dimension must be the block count, and every block adds a model-state row.
candidates.granularity: Batches of 1,024-16,384 independent blocks per inference, each block a few KiB, with one MLState per batch; per-step work of at least ~1-10 MFLOP per block so the 190 us dispatch is under 10% of step time; the whole file must be split into that many independent segments (ratio cost: each block starts with an empty context).
candidates.expectedThroughput: Back-of-envelope: at 38 TOPS peak, a 1 MFLOP-per-byte model gives 38 MB/s at 100% utilisation; with 190 us per step and 8,192 blocks per step the step rate is bounded at ~5,000 steps/s = 41 MB/s of bytes; realistic 5-20 MB/s. That is 1-3x the speed of single-thread xz at 6 MB/s (11x ratio) and far below 16-thread xz (~100 MB/s). A one-thread SME predictor at 4.0 int8 TOPS / 2.0 fp32 TFLOP/s with zero dispatch cost, or the GPU at 14.8 fp16 TFLOP/s, is the alternative the ANE must beat.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Apple Compression LZMA (xz) encode 0.006 GB/s (6 MB/s) single thread at 10.96x on the SDK tar, decode 0.41 GB/s; GyoshukuKit's ParallelXZCompressor runs up to 64 threads of LZMA2 on 16 MiB blocks (~100 MB/s back-of-envelope on 16 cores); KaitoKit's PPMd decoder (a context-model coder, the closest CPU analogue) not measured here.
candidates.killCriterion: MLComputePlan must show the model's matmuls placed on the Neural Engine (an LSTM that falls to GPU is not an ANE result), and the measured ANE bytes/second at equal ratio must exceed the same model run one-thread on SME (4.0 int8 TOPS measured, no dispatch cost) by at least the ratio of their dispatch overheads; if a 16-thread xz run beats both on the speed-ratio Pareto front for the corpus, the candidate is a demo only.

candidates.name: GPU byte-predictor via Metal 4 ML encoder or Shader ML (same neural model, GPU instead of ANE)
candidates.whatItComputes: The same byte-probability model, executed either as a whole network with MTL4MachineLearningCommandEncoder (mlpackage compiled by metal-package-builder) or as matmul2d/cooperative_tensor ops inside a custom compute kernel that also runs the range coder per block on the GPU.
candidates.mapping: Metal 4 on M4 Max supports MTLTensor (UInt8/Int8/Int32/Float16/BFloat16 and, from macOS 27, FP8/FP4/Int2 with scale planes), and MPP matmul2d compiles here for int8->int32, half and bfloat inputs; but M4 Max has no neural accelerators (those arrive with M5/A19), so tensor ops run on the ordinary shader ALUs at a measured 14.8 fp16 TFLOP/s (Rigel), and MPP beats simdgroup_matrix by only 1.05-1.21x. The advantage over the ANE is that the range coder and the model can share one kernel with no per-step dispatch (a threadgroup per block loops over bytes), removing the 165 us per step; the disadvantage is 32 KiB threadgroup memory for weights (a 256x256 fp16 layer is 128 KiB, so weights stream from device memory each step).
candidates.granularity: Thousands of independent blocks (one simdgroup or threadgroup each) resident for the whole kernel; model under ~1 M parameters so weights stay L2-resident; per-block serial loop over bytes inside the kernel.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Back-of-envelope: 14.8 TFLOP/s / 1 MFLOP per byte = 14.8 MB/s at 100% utilisation; realistic 3-10 MB/s at 20-60% utilisation, similar to the ANE estimate but without the batching constraint on dispatch count. Same league as single-thread xz (6 MB/s), far below 16-thread xz.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Same as the ANE candidate: xz 6 MB/s 1T at 11x; GyoshukuKit parallel xz ~100 MB/s (back-of-envelope); one SME thread at 4.0 int8 TOPS / 2.0 fp32 TFLOP/s (measured) running the same model.
candidates.killCriterion: If the GPU kernel's bytes/second at equal ratio does not exceed a one-thread SME implementation of the same model by more than ~3x (the GPU has ~7x the fp16 FLOP/s of one SME thread's fp32 but pays for serial per-block loops), the CPU-coprocessor path is preferable and the GPU version is a demo only.
candidates.firstExperiment: Compile a Metal 4 kernel that runs a 2-layer 128-unit MLP per block with mpp::tensor_ops::matmul2d<execution_simdgroups<1>> and an in-kernel binary arithmetic coder over 4 KiB blocks for 8,192 blocks; verify decode equals encode input on the CPU; report bytes/second and compare with the ANE and SME numbers.

candidates.name: SME (matrix coprocessor) for context-model / neural predictor arithmetic on the CPU
candidates.whatItComputes: Outer-product accumulation into ZA tiles (svmopa) for the dot-product-heavy parts of a compressor that already runs on the CPU: logistic mixing in PPMd/CM-style coders, or the matmuls of a small byte predictor, executed by the thread that also runs the range coder, with no dispatch boundary.
candidates.mapping: FEAT_SME/SME2 with SME_I8I32, SME_F32F32, F64F64 are present (sysctl), SVL is 512 bits, and a plain C file with arm_sme.h intrinsics runs from user space today (clang -march=armv8.7-a+sme2; armv9 -march values SIGILL because the compiler prologue emits non-streaming SVE cntd and M4 has SME without SVE). The unit is shared per cluster, so throughput does not scale with thread count. It does nothing for byte-level LZ, CRC, Huffman or AES work: there is no gather, no table lookup, and no LUT instruction (FEAT_SME_LUTv2 = 0). Accelerate's BNNS/vDSP/BLAS are the supported front door and are float/NN shaped; vImageHistogramCalculation_Planar8 is the only byte-level Accelerate primitive relevant to compression.
candidates.granularity: Matrix tiles of 16x16 fp32 or 16x64 int8 per instruction; useful only when a predictor has >=64-wide dot products per byte (below that NEON is as fast); the streaming-mode entry/exit around each call costs tens of cycles, so batch many bytes per streaming region.
candidates.expectedThroughput: Measured one thread: 1.93 G svmopa_za32_s8/s = 1.98 TMAC/s = 4.0 int8 TOPS; 3.88 G svmopa_za32_f32/s = 1.99 fp32 TFLOP/s (loop over 4 ZA tiles, register-resident inputs; memory-bound real models will be lower). For a 1 MFLOP-per-byte model that is ~2-4 MB/s per thread at ideal utilisation, i.e. the same league as the ANE/GPU estimates for the same model.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: NEON on the same thread (roughly 8-16 fp32 FMA per cycle per core, ~0.1-0.3 TFLOP/s; unmeasured here), and the existing KaitoKit PPMd/LZMA and GyoshukuKit LZMA2 coders (unmeasured here).
candidates.killCriterion: If the predictor's dot products are narrower than ~64 elements or the model is memory-bound (weights not L1/L2 resident), NEON matches SME and the streaming-mode overhead loses; also, one SME unit per cluster means a 12-thread CPU predictor gains at most ~3x from SME (3 clusters), which must be verified with a 12-thread run.
candidates.firstExperiment: Extend sme6.c to a 256x256 fp16/int8 GEMV per byte streamed from L2 (weights 64-128 KiB), measure bytes/second on one thread, then on 12 threads to observe the per-cluster sharing; compare with the same model on the GPU and the ANE.

candidates.name: MPSGraph for byte-level elementwise work (bitwise ops, gather, histogram-like reductions)
candidates.whatItComputes: Graph-level elementwise ops on UInt8/Int32 tensors: bitwiseAND/OR/XOR/NOT, left/right shift, population count, gather/gatherND/gatherAlongAxis, scatterND, cumulative ops, sort, topK, nonZero, plus matmul; runs on the GPU through MPSGraphExecutable.
candidates.mapping: The op set is enough to express CRC-free checksums (e.g. Adler-32 style sums), delta/XOR filters (7z BCJ/delta-like), byte transposition and histogram via one-hot+reduce, all without writing MSL; MPSDataTypeUInt8/Int32/Bool exist. It cannot express a serial decoder loop, a range coder or LZ77 parsing, and each graph run is a full GPU dispatch (>=165 us) with tensor allocation, so it only helps for whole-buffer elementwise passes that are not already memory-bound on the CPU (memcpy 69 GB/s per core; XOR loop 48 GB/s per core).
candidates.granularity: Whole buffers of tens of MiB per graph run; static shapes preferred (recompiles otherwise).
candidates.expectedThroughput: Bounded by GPU bandwidth (311 GB/s measured read) minus graph overhead; for a fused XOR/shift pass expect 100-200 GB/s on 256 MiB (back-of-envelope), i.e. 2-4x one CPU core and roughly parity with 16 cores for trivially vectorised filters.
candidates.cpuBaselineToBeat: Single-core 64-bit XOR loop 47.8 GB/s, memcpy 69 GB/s, histogram 4.8 GB/s 1T / 38 GB/s 16T (measured); KaitoKit SevenZipFilters (BCJ/delta) not measured.
candidates.killCriterion: If a fused MPSGraph elementwise pass on 256 MiB is not faster than 16 CPU threads on the same filter (for XOR/delta that is >~500 GB/s back-of-envelope, above GPU bandwidth), the candidate is dead; it survives only for compute-heavier per-byte transforms that are not expressible in NEON efficiently, of which the archive codecs have none.
candidates.firstExperiment: Build an MPSGraph that takes a UInt8 [N] tensor, computes bitwiseXOR with a shifted copy (a 1-byte delta filter) and a 256-bin histogram via oneHot+reductionSum, run on 256 MiB, time the run and compare with the C XOR loop and the histogram bars.

facts.fact: Apple Neural Engine facts: exposed to apps only through Core ML; datapath is fp16 end to end (fp32/int32/bf16 accepted by the frontend but not implemented; int8/int4/palette weights reconstruct to fp16 before the multiply array); executes a static graph, no data-dependent control flow, no integer bitwise ops or gather; a tiny graph dispatched in a hot loop costs ~190 us per call with ~98% software/firmware overhead (kernel user-client submit ~163 us); M1 slope ~12 fp16 TFLOP/s against an ~85 GB/s DRAM ceiling; direct measurements were on M1 and M5, not M4.

facts.fact: Repository granularity: GyoshukuKit ParallelXZCompressor cuts tar input into 16 MiB blocks (LZMA2ChunkPipeline.chunkSize 16 MiB, memberPackingSize 4 MiB, lightChunkLimit 64 KiB) each encoded independently on up to 64 threads; ParallelBzip2Compressor uses chunks of 5 x level x 100,000 bytes; ZipAESEncryptor builds little-endian counters, encrypts them with ECB via CCCrypt per IOChunk, XORs per byte in Swift and HMAC-SHA1s the ciphertext. KaitoKit decodes XZ through a single Apple Compression stream (no block parallelism), decodes zstd serially, parallelises bzip2 only at byte-aligned stream starts (max 8 workers, 8 MiB compressed / 16 MiB output per interval), reads the LZ4 frame block-independence flag (flags & 32) and keeps 64 KiB history for dependent blocks, uses zlib for CRC-32 and Deflate, CommonCrypto ECB for WinZip AES and CBC random access for 7z/RAR.

risks: Measurements were taken while other agents and builds may have been running on the same machine (the plan's own noise rule); rerun bars.c/aes2.c/gpubw.swift/hist.swift alone before quoting numbers in the speed report.
The CRC 12-thread figure came from a run whose N/12 chunking left a remainder (value mismatch); only the 16-thread 238 GB/s number is an exact-match measurement.

The CPU bars measured are Apple Compression, zlib and CommonCrypto; KaitoKit's own Swift decoders (LZMA/LZMA2, PPMd, RAR, Deflate64, Zstd, LZ4, StuffIt) and GyoshukuKit's Swift LZMA2/LH5 encoders were not measured and may be slower, which would flatter any GPU comparison unless the report says which baseline it beats.
GPU dispatch cost (127-165 us) and 32-bit-only atomics constrain every GPU candidate; any design that needs per-block CPU round trips or 64-bit counters must be re-planned.
Encrypted-archive candidates are bounded by serial stages (HMAC-SHA1 3.1 GB/s for ZIP AE-2, AES-CBC encrypt 1.8 GB/s for 7z/RAR); a GPU AES win would not show in end-to-end wall.

ANE int8 support on M4 is contested between coremltools documentation (int8-int8 path on M4) and the ANE architecture guide (int8 reconstructs to fp16; measured on M1/M5); the 190 us dispatch figure is from M1, so M4 Max values must be measured with MLComputePlan placement recorded per op.

Neural-compression candidates land in the 3-40 MB/s range at best, competitive with single-thread xz (6 MB/s) but far below GyoshukuKit's multi-threaded xz; they can win on ratio, not on wall, and a one-thread SME predictor (4.0 int8 TOPS, no dispatch) is a cheaper CPU alternative that must be beaten.

SME compile fragility: -march=armv9.x flags produce SIGILL binaries on M4 (SVE prologue); Swift has no SME intrinsics, so SME code must live in a C target compiled with -march=armv8.7-a+sme2, and the unit is shared per cluster.

Block-parallel GPU decode requires independent units the archive formats often lack (Deflate has no block index, bzip2 blocks are bit-aligned, LZMA2 chunks share a dictionary, LZ4 independence is a per-frame flag); the cheaper competitor is a CPU multi-block reader, which KaitoKit does not have for XZ or zstd today.

Several external numbers (GPULZ/nvCOMP GB/s, Weissenberger/Yamamoto throughput, Geekbench M1 AES-XTS, Eclectic Light hardware claim) come from search snippets or blocked pages and are marked unverified; do not cite them as facts in the technology document without fetching the primary source.
powermetrics tracing of GPU/ANE power during an LZFSE run (needs sudo) was not performed; it is the remaining check for the 'no hardware compression engine' conclusion.

missingKillCriteria: gpu-compression LZ4 block-parallel decode: the kill is written for a 1 GB frame of 64 KiB blocks that no writer in this ecosystem produces (GyoshukuKit writes no LZ4; lz4 CLI default is 4 MiB blocks, measured), so the realistic 4 MiB-block input (256 blocks/GiB, expected 2-8 GB/s) has no kill criterion at all; the 25 GB/s bar is also unverified and depends on which LZ4 CPU number is used (2.58 vs 2.85 vs 5.33 GB/s per core across angles).

gpu-compression Zstd GPU decode: the kill ('one threadgroup per block below 20 GB/s') rests on a false premise: zstd blocks within a frame share the window and are not independent; only frames are (pzstd / seekable format). The candidate needs a criterion of the form 'input has >= N independent frames' or it is dead by format, not by measurement.

codec-stage-map bzip2 GPU variant: the kill compares GPU aggregate against a 12-core CPU block decoder that does not exist (libbz2 cannot start mid-stream; an own Swift block decoder with bit-level magic scan is required), so the criterion cannot be tested without first building the competitor; the CPU per-block time it references was never measured (only 50 MB/s serial).

codec-stage-map GPU exhaustive LH5 match finding: no ratio criterion, and 'byte identical to CPU path' is undefined because exhaustive matching changes the output relative to the 256-probe hash chain; the kill must name a CPU reference implementing the same exhaustive rule and a minimum ratio gain that justifies the different bytes.

codec-stage-map GPU Deflate match finding: the kill ('CPU emitter slower than ~120 MB/s per core') requires a Swift Deflate Huffman emitter that does not exist; the prerequisite build is unstated and gpu-compression declares the same candidate already dead ('no encoder accepts external matches'). One of the two verdicts must be adopted.

apple-platform ANE byte predictor: 'must exceed the same model on one SME thread by at least the ratio of their dispatch overheads' is not a number; and the SME comparison baseline (a working SME predictor) does not exist. Replace with a bytes/s and ratio pair on a named corpus.

GPU forward BWT: two incompatible thresholds (gpu-compression kill < 300 MB/s including remaining stages; codec-stage-map kill < 200 MB/s aggregate) and two incompatible statuses (gpu-compression: blocked by closed libbz2; codec-stage-map: live with own Swift MTF/RLE/Huffman). Also both depend on an unmeasured blocksort share.

apple-platform GPU byte histogram: recommended as first experiment yet its own kill (frequency counting < 5% of encode wall) is expected to be met; also nothing in either repository consumes a raw byte histogram (LH5 and Deflate build Huffman tables over LZ command symbols, not input bytes). Needs a criterion tied to a consumer or it is a primitive demo only.

apple-platform SME candidate: kill depends on a NEON baseline nobody measured and on 'one SME unit per cluster', which was only inferred from single-thread runs; the 12-thread SME scaling test is the missing criterion.

Three neural ratio kills on three corpora: ane-coreml (beat 7zz PPMd o6 ratio 5.25 on an 11.4 MB Swift/Markdown corpus with <= 1M params), neural-lossless (beat PPMd o32 21.92% on a held-out enwik9 slice with <= 3M params, <= 4 GPU-hours), codec-stage-map (ratio < 0.28 on synthetic text256). They are not the same test; text256 is MT19937-generated dictionary words so a model trained on it is rigged. One held-out real-text corpus and one PPMd order must be fixed.

No GPU decode kill (LZ4, bzip2, zstd, Deflate) includes malformed-input safety: a kernel without bounds guards is not comparable to KaitoKit's hardened decoders; each kill should require the guarded kernel's throughput, not the unguarded one.

No decode candidate has a sink-side criterion: a decode faster than the consumer (SSD write ~5-7 GB/s, SHA-256 3 GB/s/core, KaitoFinder extraction) cannot show in wall time; kills should state the end-to-end path measured.

Apple Compression hardware offload: the stated kill (powermetrics gpu_power/ane_power during a 1 GiB LZFSE encode showing zero) was not run; it needs sudo and should be scheduled, not left as 'effectively killed'.

CPU scaling: gpu-compression asserts multi-core scaling is 'well below 16x' from the xz -T16 run, while apple-platform and codec-stage-map multiply single-thread rates by 12-16; the xz run was block-limited, so neither position is measured.
gaps: Zstd block dependence: no angle states that zstd blocks (128 KiB) share the frame window, so 'one threadgroup per block' is impossible for standard zstd output; only multi-frame outputs (pzstd, seekable format) are block-parallel. KaitoKit's zstd path and GyoshukuKit (which writes no zstd) were not checked for multi-frame handling.

GyoshukuKit-written 7z: LZMA2 is encoded per 16 MiB chunk via compression_encode_buffer and re-framed, so each chunk should begin with a dictionary reset; nobody scanned a GyoshukuKit 7z with codecmap-count.py. KaitoKit could block-parallel-decode its sibling's 7z and tar.xz (16 MiB blocks) output, a larger CPU win than the 7zz-written text.7z (1 reset) suggests.

Block-parallel bzip2 on the CPU: codec-stage-map names it but no one plans the own Swift bzip2 block decoder with bit-level magic scan (299 bit-aligned blocks in text.tar.bz2 vs 1 byte-aligned start); it is the cheaper competitor every GPU bzip2 candidate must beat and the fix for the 50 MB/s serial path on ordinary .bz2 files.

Sink bandwidth: no angle states the consumer limit of decoded bytes (SSD write ~5-7 GB/s, SHA-256 3 GB/s per core, KaitoFinder extraction workers <= 8); any decode above ~5 GB/s is invisible end-to-end, which bounds the value of every GPU decode candidate independent of GPU speed.

MTLIO (Metal 3 fast resource loading) inline decompression of LZ4/LZFSE/zlib/LZMA was cited by two angles but not measured; decoding a 256 MiB LZ4 file through MTLIOCommandQueue while sampling CPU time is the direct test of 'does Apple decompress off the CPU', cheaper than powermetrics and needing no sudo.
LZBitmap (COMPRESSION_LZBITMAP, the Apple codec designed for fast decode on Apple silicon) and libParallelCompression (AppleArchive's multithreaded path) were named but never measured or inspected.

Pipelined Metal throughput: only commit-to-completion round trip (146-165 us) was measured; the per-dispatch cost with several command buffers in flight, which is what a batched decode pipeline pays, is unknown.

Zero-copy tax: makeBuffer(bytesNoCopy:) needs 16 KiB-aligned pages; KaitoKit 256 KiB / GyoshukuKit 1 MiB Data buffers are not aligned, so every GPU candidate pays a memcpy (~73 GB/s => ~14 ms per GiB) or an allocator change; flagged as a risk by codec-stage-map, measured by nobody.

KaitoKit's own Swift decoders (LZ4, LZMA2, zstd 197 MB/s, Deflate64, RAR, LHA) have no MB/s on a common corpus; every GPU comparison so far is against libcompression/zlib/libbz2, not the code that ships. `kaito bench` exists and was not run by any angle.

Energy and offload framing: GPU/ANE work at CPU parity that leaves the CPU idle (neural-lossless measured CPU ~80% idle during ANE steps) may matter for a GUI archiver on battery; no angle measured joules per GB (powermetrics) or framed GPU value as offload rather than speed.

Runtime ANE proof for neural-lossless: its latency numbers rest on static MLComputePlan only; ane-coreml showed a floor model with static 'ANE' placement can still produce zero ANE hardware intervals, so neural-lossless's GRU numbers need xctrace confirmation.

Fixed batch baked into MLState shape and the tail problem (padding or a second model), plus the >= B x 2 KiB input granularity (8 MiB at B=4096), are noted as risks but no experiment measures the small-archive cliff that a GUI archiver would hit on typical inputs.
xz's own parallel decoder (`xz -d -T16`, available since 5.4.1) on text.tar.xz gives the multi-core XZ bar in minutes; no angle ran it before estimating the CPU block-parallel win.

GDeflate-style writer-controlled interleaving (GyoshukuKit emitting 32-substream Deflate or 64 KiB LZ4 blocks) was mentioned only as a contrast; its interoperability cost (foreign readers) was never weighed against the parallelism gain, which is the only path to >20k independent streams.
Perf hygiene: all five angles measured on a shared, possibly loaded machine; no angle established a base-vs-base noise floor for the GPU or ANE timings, which plan.md requires before any claim.

Corpus: five angles used five corpora (719 MB source concat; 11.4 MB Swift/Markdown; enwik8; scratchpad text256/small/headers; 34 MiB SDK-headers tar). The plan has no agreed corpus, so no cross-angle number can be compared or reused as a kill denominator.
recommendedFirstExperiments: 1. On an idle machine, with base-vs-base noise floor and alternating medians, run KaitoAccelLab baseline plus `kaito bench` on the kk2 perf corpus (text.tar.gz/xz/bz2/zst, text.7z, a 1 GiB lz4-CLI frame) to record CRC-32, AES-CTR, libcompression LZ4 1-thread and 16-lane, and KaitoKit's own LZ4/zstd/LZMA2/bzip2 decoders: expect CRC ~41-47 GB/s per core and ~240 GB/s on 16 lanes, AES-CTR 14-18 GB/s per core, 16-lane LZ4 far below 16x (memory-bound, 20-40 GB/s), and KaitoKit's Swift decoders slower than the reference libraries; this fixes every kill denominator on one corpus and decides whether the real gap is CPU port quality rather than hardware.

2. Write a real LZ4 block decoder in MSL and measure one GPU thread on one 64 KiB and one 4 MiB block against one P-core, then a warp-cooperative (32 lanes for literal/match copies) variant, then full occupancy on the 1 GiB frame (16,384 x 64 KiB and 256 x 4 MiB), reporting aggregate = min(blocks, resident threads) x per-block rate with bounds guards on: expect 5-30 MB/s per lone thread, 50-200 MB/s per warp-block, 1-10 GB/s aggregate for 64 KiB blocks and under 2 GB/s for 4 MiB blocks, below the 16-lane libcompression bar from experiment 1; this kills or confirms GPU block-parallel decode in one shot, and GPU bzip2/zstd decode die with it if the per-block rate is where the table-lookup probe says.

3. Run `xz -d -T16` on text.tar.xz (11 blocks) and `xz -lvv` plus a codecmap-count.py scan of a GyoshukuKit-written 7z and tar.xz to count dictionary resets, then prototype KaitoKit block-parallel XZ decode with its own LZMA2Decoder: expect xz -T16 around 1.0-1.4 GB/s (3-4x over 322 MB/s), the GyoshukuKit 7z to show one reset per 16 MiB chunk, and the prototype to cut text.tar.xz from 1.9 s to 0.3-0.5 s; this decides whether the largest user-visible win is CPU-only and sets the multi-core bar that any GPU XZ attempt must beat.

4. Measure MTLIO inline decompression of the 256 MiB LZ4 and LZFSE files through MTLIOCommandQueue while sampling CPU time, and have the owner run `sudo powermetrics --samplers gpu_power,ane_power,cpu_power` during a 1 GiB LZFSE encode/decode: expect MTLIO at CPU-thread rates with matching CPU time and zero GPU/ANE power during Apple Compression; this closes the 'does Apple use non-CPU hardware for compression' question as measured rather than inferred from dyld linkage.

5. Profile with Instruments (Time Profiler) bzip2 -9 / libbz2 compress for the blocksort share and GyoshukuKit's LH5Encoder and DeflateBlock (zlib -6) for the match-finding share on text256, and measure the memcpy tax of staging 1 MiB non-page-aligned Data blocks into a bytesNoCopy MTLBuffer: expect blocksort 50-70% (so a free GPU BWT caps at 2-3x on a closed encoder), LH5 hash-chain matching above 80% of encode time, and ~14 ms per GiB copy tax; this decides that the only encode-side GPU demo worth building is the LH5 match finder with a CPU exhaustive-rule reference, and kills GPU BWT and Deflate matching without writing new encoders.

6. Build one Swift harness that runs ane-coreml's MLState LSTM cell and neural-lossless's GRU at B=1024/4096 with fp16 inputs, a 32-bit range coder over 2048-byte blocks, xctrace Core AI ane-hw-intervals proof, a batch-position-invariance check under MLState, and a 12-thread BNNS/Accelerate CPU run of the same fp16 model on enwik8: expect 1.5-4 MB/s symmetric round trip on the ANE, ANE and CPU outputs differing at the 1e-3 level (archives bound to the ANE path), and the 12-thread CPU run reaching 3-7 MB/s; this decides whether the ANE has any speed edge at all (kill (a)) before spending GPU-hours on the ratio training that is the only remaining justification (kill (b) against PPMd o32 on a held-out enwik9 slice).
critique.verdict: The five angles agree on the negatives and disagree on the one positive that is left. Agreed and adequately measured on this machine: GPU CRC-32 and AES can at best tie the 16-lane CPU (238-243 GB/s and 114-142 GB/s against a 311-369 GB/s GPU ceiling), so they are 'why the CPU wins' sections, not candidates; the ANE runs a byte predictor at 1.5-4 MB/s, beats Core ML's own CPU path by only 1.2-1.8x, is fp16 and non-bit-identical across compute units, and can only be a ratio demo; range coders (LZMA, PPMd, RAR) and single-stream Deflate offer no GPU parallelism; encode-side offload is blocked by closed encoders except for the in-house LH5 encoder; block count, not per-block speed, binds every block-parallel decode. Not settled: GPU block-parallel LZ4 decode is simultaneously the recommended first GPU experiment (gpu-compression, 10-40 GB/s from an unverified RTX 3090 number), 'no gain expected' (codec-stage-map), and near-killed by apple-platform's per-thread rule, because the two angles use incompatible lane models and neither measured real LZ4 per-block work on the GPU; the kill criterion is also written for a 64 KiB-block frame nobody in this ecosystem writes. The zstd GPU candidate rests on a false independence assumption. The neural demo has three different ratio kills on three corpora, one of them a synthetic dictionary-word corpus that would rig the result, and only one angle has runtime (xctrace) proof of ANE execution. Five corpora and three PPMd baselines make the angles' numbers non-comparable, and no angle established the noise floor plan.md requires.
